steps: Confirm the indication

Proceed only after maximal nonsurgical therapy leaves a meaningful functional voice limitation. Review a recent stroboscopy (ideally within about 2–3 weeks) on the day of surgery so the lesion location, wave impairment, and planned incision can be correlated with operative findings.
Counsel and prepare

Stop aspirin, NSAIDs, and anticoagulants; avoid heavy voice use beforehand and avoid scheduling in the premenstrual phase. Consent for dental, TMJ, and lingual nerve injury (usually temporary) and a small (about 1–2%) chance of no improvement or worse voice; a preoperative voice therapy session sets up voice rest.
Anesthesia and airway

General anesthesia with full paralysis, IV dexamethasone (10–20 mg) and glycopyrrolate. Intubate gently under surgeon observation with a small (5.0–5.5) microlaryngeal tube, ideally without a stylet, so the fold is not traumatized before surgery.
Position the patient

Supine with the neck flexed on the chest and the head extended on the neck (raise the articulated head of the table or use a pillow). Do not use a shoulder roll, which extends the neck and makes exposure worse. Place a maxillary tooth guard.
Expose with the largest scope

Insert the largest-bore laryngoscope that will show the entire membranous fold; slide behind the tube along the posterior pharyngeal wall and lift into the larynx if the epiglottis folds. Seat the tip just above the lesion, retracting the false fold without pressing on the true fold.
Suspend and optimize

Suspend (gallows preferred; with a fulcrum device protect the upper incisors, since tip elevation transmits equal force onto the alveolus). Add external cricoid counterpressure with tape if needed and position the table so the scope sits low in the seated surgeon's lap.
Telescope and palpate

Inspect with 0, 30, and 70 degree long rod telescopes to map the lesion, ventricle, and subglottis. Palpate both folds with a blunt instrument to feel the lesion depth and confirm a microflap is appropriate, then bring the 400-mm microscope in at maximal magnification.
Subepithelial infusion

For a suspected cyst or fibrous mass, inject 1:10,000 epinephrine just posterior and lateral to the lesion with a 27-gauge orotracheal injector. This hydrodissects the subepithelial plane and improves hemostasis; it is not used for polyps because it blurs the lesion margin.
Make the cordotomy

Use a fresh sickle knife to make a superficial incision on the superior surface just lateral to the lesion, slightly longer than the lesion. Tent the epithelium upward as you cut so the blade does not enter the cyst or deeper layers; avoid incising directly over a cyst.
Dissect medially first

With a 30 degree flap elevator, develop the plane between the thin epithelial cover and the lesion, starting in undisturbed tissue anterior and posterior to it. Finish this medial dissection before the deep side, because the lesion's attachment to the ligament provides countertraction.
Free the lesion from the ligament

Retract the flap with triangular forceps and dissect the lesion off the white, longitudinally oriented vocal ligament with an angled elevator, using microscissors for fibrous bands at the anterior and posterior poles. Stay superficial and keep any residual gelatinous superficial lamina propria.
Protect the cyst wall

Handle the cyst gently; if punctured, grasp the opening with a microalligator to keep it from collapsing and complete removal while the wall is visible. Ligament-level lesions elevate easily superficially but require careful deep dissection and have slower recovery.
Hemostasis and inspection

Control oozing with small 1:10,000 epinephrine pledgets and a 3-French suction without occluding the thumb port. Remove the lesion intact, redrape the flap, and re-palpate; the free edge should be straight with no residual mass, mucosal tag, or defect.
Finish conservatively

Do not excise redundant epithelium routinely. Optionally inject dexamethasone (10 mg/mL) superficially at the site to limit scar, apply topical lidocaine, and coordinate a smooth extubation without coughing.
Postoperative care

About 1 week of complete voice rest, then stroboscopy; if the epithelium has covered, start light breathy voice use for 5–10 minutes per hour and graduated voice therapy. Continue reflux treatment if indicated; antibiotics and long steroid courses are rarely needed.

steps: Set the goal

RRP recurs in almost all patients and many undergo dozens of procedures, so aim to restore airway and voice with minimal scar or web, not to achieve complete eradication. Operate for diagnosis, airway, or voice symptoms rather than visible disease alone.
Avoid tracheotomy
Work to prevent tracheotomy, which creates a new squamous-ciliated junction where papilloma seeds and greatly complicates care.
Equipment and safety

Have the phonomicrosurgery set, a microdebrider with a conservative skimmer blade, and CO2 and/or pulsed KTP lasers. When lasers are used, apply full laser safety: laser-resistant tube, low FiO2, wet protection of the face and adjacent mucosa.
Expose and map

Use the largest laryngoscope, repositioning as needed, and map the disease with 30 and 70 degree telescopes, including the ventricles, anterior commissure, subglottis, and posterior commissure (displace the tube to see it).
Infuse beneath disease
Inject epinephrine subepithelially beneath the planned area; this hydrodissects papilloma from the lamina propria, medializes superior-surface disease for viewing, and improves hemostasis.
Microflap for first diagnosis

At the first procedure, a microflap excision just lateral to the disease gives a full-thickness specimen; no margin is needed. In later operations scarred planes make this technique risky for the ligament.
Cold forceps for focal disease

Grasp only the superficial papilloma with 1–2 mm cup or ovoid forceps and avulse with an up or down pull, never anterior-posterior, which strips adjacent mucosa. Alternating two forceps with an assistant speeds removal.
Microdebrider technique

Use the 2.9-mm skimmer blade at a low speed (about 800–1200 rpm), holding the port just above disease. Modulate suction with a figure-of-eight loop of tubing and pin the fold with a blunt probe so the ligament is not drawn in; collect tissue in an inline trap.
CO2 laser technique

Use a defocused spot of about 0.5–0.75 mm at low power (2–4 W) in intermittent superpulse, or a pattern scanner. Keep the beam moving so no spot is hit repeatedly, and clear char with 5- or 7-French suction.
Pulsed KTP technique

Hold the fiber 1–2 mm off superficial disease until it blanches (KTP-1), then wipe or suction it away, leaving intact tissue. Bulky disease needs contact treatment with frequent reassessment of depth to avoid lamina propria loss.
Protect the anterior commissure

Remove disease from one side of the anterior commissure at a time, first making a cut through the papilloma at the midline. With bilateral disease, debulk the worse side and treat the other only to a KTP-1 effect.
Respect subglottis and posterior glottis
Use cold steel or microdebrider in the subglottis, with conservative low-power CO2 if exposure is poor; stage posterior commissure work unilaterally to avoid posterior glottic stenosis.
Adjuvant cidofovir

If used, inject cidofovir (about 2.5–5 mg/mL; higher concentrations scar) superficially with a 25–27 gauge needle in a caudal-to-cephalad sequence: subglottis, posterior commissure, free edges, superior surfaces and ventricles, false folds. Repeat monthly for three or more sessions; bevacizumab is an alternative.
Final inspection and follow-up

Re-examine with angled telescopes to confirm gross disease is removed, achieve hemostasis with pledgets, and schedule interval surveillance. Many patients can alternate operating room sessions with awake office KTP treatment.

steps: Select injection vs framework

Injection suits temporary correction while recovery is uncertain, trial augmentation when the contribution of glottic insufficiency is unclear, and small gaps (under about 1 mm). Gaps of 2–3 mm or more, or a large posterior gap, are better served by medialization with or without arytenoid adduction.
Choose the material

Match duration to the goal: gelatin about 4–6 weeks, carboxymethylcellulose about 6–8 weeks, micronized dermis about 2–3 months, hyaluronic acid about 3–4 months or longer, calcium hydroxylapatite about 9–12 months, and fat potentially years. Teflon is no longer appropriate because of delayed granulomas.
Prepare awake anesthesia

For office injection, decongest and anesthetize the nose, spray the oropharynx, and drip 4% lidocaine onto the larynx during phonation through a curved cannula or scope channel, or nebulize it. Keep the total within about 4.5 mg/kg (roughly 7–8 mL of 4% in a 70-kg adult).
Position and monitor

Seat the patient upright, leaning forward in the sniffing position, with an assistant holding a distal-chip flexible laryngoscope (usually through the nostril opposite the injected side) displaying the larynx on a monitor. Prime the needle with injectate so no air is injected.
Per-oral route

Pass a curved 24–27 gauge transoral injector through the mouth in the midline while the tongue is held forward, following it into the larynx under endoscopic view. This route gives direct needle visualization and suits most materials.
Transthyroid or cricothyroid route

Alternatively pass a 23–25 gauge needle through the thyroid ala about 6–12 mm from midline at the estimated vocal fold level, or below the thyroid cartilage through the cricothyroid membrane angled up. Do not overshoot into the airway once through cartilage.
Thyrohyoid route

Or enter just above the thyroid notch, angled steeply down, traversing the pre-epiglottic space to emerge at the petiole; the tip is visible on the monitor, which makes it easy to learn. A double-bent needle improves reach to the posterior fold.
Target the deep lateral plane

Inject lateral within the thyroarytenoid at the level of the vocal process along the superior arcuate line (junction of the superior surface and ventricle), about 3–5 mm deep, angled laterally. Avoid superficial deposit in Reinke space, which stiffens the fold.
Inject in stages

For paralysis, start at the posterior site lateral to the vocal process where most correction is needed, then add a smaller amount at the mid-membranous fold. For bowing from atrophy or paresis, inject mainly at the mid-fold. Withdraw slightly if the subglottis starts to bulge.
Titrate to voice and view

Inject stepwise while checking the voice and closure. Once the voice is maximal, add about 0.1–0.2 mL to overcorrect slightly, since the aqueous carrier resorbs within days; most unilateral injections total under 1 mL. A firm cough can smooth a focal bulge.
Microlaryngoscopy variant

Under general anesthesia, suspend a large laryngoscope angled toward the injected side and inject at the same landmarks; there is no voice endpoint, so judge contour visually and overcorrect according to material. Spray 3–4 mL of 4% lidocaine afterward to reduce laryngospasm.
Lipoinjection specifics

Fat is injected under general anesthesia with a pressurized syringe. Harvest by low-pressure, large-cannula liposuction or open infraumbilical excision, wash away free fatty acids and blood, and overinject generously because early resorption is variable.
Manage misplacement

If material goes superficial or into the subglottis, milk it out with lateral pressure from a cannula or enlarge the puncture; long-lasting material in Reinke space may need removal under microlaryngoscopy because it can persist 6–18 months.
Aftercare

Observe briefly for airway compromise, keep the patient NPO for about 1–2 hours until sensation returns, and use no more than about 24 hours of voice rest. The voice is best at 1–2 weeks. Watch for a hyaluronic acid inflammatory reaction at 2–3 days, treated with a steroid taper.

steps: Confirm diagnosis and timing

Offer permanent glottic widening for symptomatic airway obstruction in long-standing paralysis (about 9–12 months), sooner if LEMG predicts no recovery. Distinguish paralysis from posterior glottic stenosis or joint fixation, and avoid destructive surgery in rapidly progressive neurologic disease, which is usually managed with tracheotomy.
Set expectations

Explain that every widening procedure trades some voice and possibly swallowing for airway; patients wanting both a normal voice and normal airway are poor candidates. Aspiration, poor pulmonary reserve, and prior radiation are relative contraindications.
Choose the side
Operate on the less mobile fold; if neither moves, use LEMG and arytenoid palpation to pick the side with the worst neuromuscular function and joint mechanics.
Palpate the joints

With the patient paralyzed and ideally no tube in place, keep the laryngoscope above the larynx and move each arytenoid (or press the muscular process medially from the piriform side) to grade passive mobility.
Airway and exposure

Ventilate with a 5.0–5.5 laser-safe tube kept posterior or moved anterior, or with a subglottic jet catheter. Angle the laryngoscope toward the operative side to see the lateral true and false folds, and apply full laser safety.
Protect below
Place a platform suction and moist cottonoid below the glottis to protect the subglottis and tube cuff.
Begin the cordotomy

Confirm the vocal process by palpation and, with CO2 at about 4 W superpulse with a small spot (or a scanner), cut just anterior to the vocal process to separate the fold from it without exposing cartilage, which causes granulation.
Extend laterally

Carry the cut laterally 3–4 mm into the false fold musculature until flush with the subglottic wall; expect a branch of the superior laryngeal artery, controlled with suction-bipolar cautery. Wipe char away often, since the laser does not cut through char or blood.
Titrate the opening

Check with 0 and 30 degree telescopes. The goal is a posterior glottic notch; a gain of only 2–3 mm usually gives a large airway benefit with mild voice change. Repeat procedures are preferable to over-resection.
Medial arytenoidectomy option

Alternatively vaporize a 2–3 mm strip of the medial arytenoid behind the vocal process (small spot, 2–4 W superpulse), preserving the vocal process and interarytenoid mucosa; extend into the vocal process and posterior fold only if more airway is needed.
Total arytenoidectomy option

For refractory cases, ablate arytenoid tissue until flush with the cricoid posteriorly and laterally, feeling for any residual overhang with a curved elevator and a 70 degree telescope, but never removing interarytenoid mucosa. Aspiration risk is highest with this option.
Suture lateralization option

For early paralysis (about the first 2 months) when recovery is possible, use an endo-extralaryngeal needle carrier to pass a 0 or 2-0 polypropylene loop below and above the posterior fold just anterior to the vocal process, then tie it over a button on the strap muscles through a small neck incision.
Finish the case
Optionally apply mitomycin C (0.4 mg/mL) for 5 minutes, spray 4% lidocaine to reduce laryngospasm, suction the stomach, and extubate smoothly.
Aftercare

Monitor the airway, treat reflux, and evaluate swallowing especially after arytenoidectomy. Granulation over exposed cartilage usually resolves. Repeat adductor botulinum toxin every 3–4 months is a nondestructive alternative for some patients.

steps: Select patients

Best for short (ideally 1–2 cm) cicatricial stenosis with an identifiable lumen and intact cartilage. External compression, tracheomalacia, and cartilage collapse are absolute contraindications; long (over 2–3 cm) stenosis or stenosis at the tracheostomy site are relative.
Plan with anesthesia

Preoxygenate with 100% oxygen for at least 5 minutes, use total intravenous anesthesia, and plan tubeless ventilation (jet, apnea, or high-flow nasal oxygen) to avoid traumatic intubation through the stenosis.
Expose

Place a tooth guard and suspend a subglottiscope (or Dedo laryngoscope) above the glottis, resting the suspension arm on a separate table rather than the chest. Start jet ventilation through the scope if needed but minimize supraglottic jetting.
Map the stenosis

Mark a 0 degree telescope at the vocal folds and at the top and bottom of the stenosis to measure the distance from the folds and the length; estimate the diameter against the telescope (about 5 mm) and inspect the distal trachea and bronchi.
Laser safety

Cover the eyes with moist pads and silk tape and wrap the head in wet towels. If a tube is used below the stenosis, use a laser-safe tube with oxygen 30% or less and a wet cottonoid over the cuff; pause jetting during firing as needed and have saline ready.
Advance past the folds
Tilt the scope down (posteriorly) to pass the folds without injuring them and seat it just above the scar; place a platform suction through the stenosis as a backstop.
Radial incisions

Make narrow CO2 radial cuts (about 4–8 W superpulse, or a scanner at about 8–10 W) through scar only, like bicycle spokes, typically at up to four positions, preserving mucosal strips between cuts. Cuts near 4 and 8 o'clock free the trachealis in circumferential tracheal stenosis; avoid deep posterior cuts toward the esophagus.
Finish distally

Advance the scope and extend incisions through the entire distal stenosis, checking with 0 and 30 degree telescopes; incomplete distal release is a common error. Wedge excisions without dilation are an alternative.
Balloon dilation

Pass the balloon under telescopic view with its proximal end at least 5 mm below the folds and outside the scope. Inflate for 30–60 seconds during apnea; typical noncompliant sizes are 12–14 mm in women and 14–16 mm in men, and larger sizes add trauma rather than benefit.
Watch for complications

Watch the chest for cough or spontaneous breathing during occlusion, which can cause postobstructive pulmonary edema. Rigid bronchoscope dilation (to about size 7 in men, 6 in women) is an alternative but risks stripping mucosa.
Steroid injection
Inject triamcinolone 40 mg/mL submucosally with a 27-gauge needle into the intact mucosal strips, ideally before making the cuts so less leaks out; methylprednisolone acetate is an alternative.
Mitomycin C
Optionally apply mitomycin C (usually 0.4 mg/mL) on a tailed cottonoid or cottonoid-wrapped tube segment for 4–5 minutes; adult evidence for benefit is weak.
Emerge without a tube
Return the patient to anesthesia with mask or laryngeal mask ventilation rather than reintubation to protect the fresh surgical site.
Aftercare

Observe overnight in a monitored setting initially (outpatient for experienced repeat patients) and get a chest radiograph for low saturation, chest pain, or crepitus. Plan serial procedures and office steroid injections; refer for open resection if recurrence is frequent.

steps: Select and counsel

Offer for early glottic cancer that can be fully exposed transorally; counsel about radiation as an equal alternative. Throat pain or otalgia suggests deeper disease than T1. Inadequate exposure, often at the anterior commissure, means changing to an open approach or radiation.
Plan the resection type

Describe resection with the European Laryngological Society cordectomy scheme: I subepithelial, II ligamental (through Reinke space and ligament), III transmuscular, IV total, V extended (Va opposite fold, Vb arytenoid, Vc subglottis, Vd ventricle), VI anterior commissure disease. Depth of invasion, not the plan, sets the final type.
Laser-safe setup
Intubate with a laser-resistant tube, fill the cuff with dyed saline, keep FiO2 low, protect the face and eyes with wet towels, and run a laser time-out.
Expose and map

Suspend the largest laryngoscope that shows the entire lesion and anterior commissure. Use 0, 30, and 70 degree telescopes and a right-angle retractor to view the ventricle, anterior commissure, and infraglottic extent.
Assess depth
Palpate and consider saline infusion: dysplasia or carcinoma in situ lifts with infusion, whereas invasive cancer to the ligament or deeper stays tethered.
Choose en bloc vs bisection
Remove small superficial cancers en bloc; bisect larger lesions through the tumor to see depth and then remove each half with an appropriate deep margin.
Outline margins
With the CO2 laser on single-fire, outline the excision about 1–2 mm around the visible tumor anteriorly, posteriorly, and laterally.
Resect lateral to medial
Cut along the lateral incision to the depth needed and peel the specimen from lateral to medial so the deep margin stays under view; avoid skiving toward the tumor.
Release the specimen
Retract the specimen medially and release the inferior edge with straight-up scissors or laser. If the specimen fills the scope, push it into the subglottis before cutting the last attachments.
Orient the specimen
Pin it on a tongue blade or foam in anatomic orientation, agreed with the pathologist, so each margin can be inked and serially sectioned.
Inspect the bed
Re-examine the defect with the microscope and angled telescopes for residual or additional abnormal mucosa.
Take separate margins
Take selected margins with cup forceps or scissors as needed; frozen sections of the small laser-altered main specimen are unreliable and generally avoided.
Hemostasis and documentation
Control bleeding with epinephrine cottonoids or defocused laser, record the resection, and draw a tumor map noting depth and problem areas.
Aftercare and surveillance

Discharge the same day in most cases with a bedside swallow check if false folds and arytenoids were spared. Follow closely with endoscopy; wait about 6–12 months before augmentation or medialization of the neocord so recurrence is not masked.

steps: Select and time

Best for moderate-severe glottic insufficiency (gap about 2–3 mm or more) with breathy voice or dysphagia. In unilateral paralysis wait about 6–9 months for recovery unless the nerve is transected, LEMG shows severe degeneration, or a malignancy makes recovery unlikely; then wait about 1 month for atrophy and bridge with injection.
Consider bilateral risk
If a mediastinal tumor could later paralyze the other side, consider alternatives, since the implant capsule may limit glottic opening even after removal.
Local anesthesia and monitoring

Infiltrate about 15 mL of 1% lidocaine with epinephrine from hyoid to cricoid on the operated side, give IV dexamethasone, and keep the patient lightly sedated and able to phonate. Place an indwelling flexible laryngoscope on a video monitor, secured to a bar over the head under a clear drape.
Expose the thyroid ala

Make a 5–6 cm horizontal crease incision at mid-thyroid level, raise subplatysmal flaps from hyoid to cricoid, divide the midline raphe, and rotate the larynx to the opposite side with a hook under the thyroid notch.
Outer perichondrium and inferior border

Raise a posteriorly based outer perichondrial flap (optional) and free the cricothyroid fibers from the inferior border, exposing it behind the muscular tubercle; ignore the tubercle's downward slope when judging the horizontal plane.
Place the window low

Outline a 6 x 13 mm window (about 5 x 10 mm in women) 3 mm above the inferior border and set back about 7 mm (men) or 5 mm (women) from the anterior midline. The vocal fold lies nearer the lower border than the midpoint; a higher window medializes the false fold, while a lower one risks strut fracture.
Confirm level if needed
Pass a fine needle through the cartilage under endoscopic view to verify the vocal fold level before cutting, without passing into the airway.
Open the window
Remove the cartilage with a 15 blade in soft cartilage or a Kerrison rongeur or drill in calcified cartilage, avoiding plunging into the paraglottic space.
Open the inner perichondrium
Remove or incise the inner perichondrium in the window to expose the thyroarytenoid fascia; leaving it intact limits the depth and precision of medialization.
Develop the paraglottic pocket

Elevate superiorly, posteriorly, and inferiorly (below the inferior strut) in the bloodless plane just superficial to the TA-LCA fascia; avoid anterior dissection, which can perforate the thin ventricular mucosa.
Measure with the depth gauge

Push the TA-LCA complex medially at the inferior part of the window while the patient counts and the team watches the monitor. Record the distance from the anterior window edge to maximal push (often 10–13 mm in men, more anterior in women) and the depth from the inner table (often 5–7 mm in men, 2–3 mm in women).
Carve the implant

Carve a firm Silastic wedge to those dimensions with square cuts, thin the superior and inferior flanges, keep the medializing face at the level of the free edge, and create the posterior slot so the implant locks on the window.
Insert and fine-tune

Insert the posteroinferior end first with toothed forceps while stabilizing the cartilage. A pressed voice suggests too much anterior medialization; a breathy voice suggests undercorrection or need for more posterior push. Adjust or recarve; invest the extra minutes.
Fix and close

Trim the implant flush, secure it around the inferior strut with 4-0 permanent sutures tied loosely, confirm hemostasis, and close perichondrium, straps, platysma, and skin; drains are usually unnecessary.
Aftercare

Observe overnight if edema is marked, elevate the head, and give steroids. Voice is poor for the first hours from edema; review at 2–4 weeks. Watch for airway edema, hematoma, and extrusion, which often follows an unrecognized ventricular mucosal tear.

steps: Select patients

Add to medialization for a large posterior gap (absent vocal process contact), a lateralized or shortened paralyzed fold, or a vertical height mismatch (usually the paralyzed fold sits high). A maximum phonation time under about 5 seconds also suggests the need.
Understand the effect
The suture mimics the lateral cricoarytenoid, pulling the muscular process forward to rotate the arytenoid, lower and medialize the vocal process, and lengthen the fold.
Begin with the medialization exposure

Expose the ala and open the medialization window as for Silastic or Gore-Tex medialization, taking preliminary depth measurements first; alternatively place the arytenoid suture before cutting the window to keep the ala stronger.
Extend the exposure posteriorly
Extend the outer perichondrial flap to the posterior border of the ala from superior to inferior cornu and connect the paraglottic pocket to the posterior border in one continuous plane.
Gain posterior access
Pass an elevator around the posterior border and open the space, then either remove a posterior window of ala or separate the cricothyroid joint and retract the ala laterally.
Protect the piriform mucosa
Identify the piriform sinus mucosa (it transilluminates when the patient blows against pursed lips) and retract it medially and upward without tearing it.
Find the muscular process
Follow the posterior cricoarytenoid fibers up and forward to their tendinous insertion on the rice-grain-sized muscular process, at about the level of the vocal fold.
Confirm by traction
Pull on the muscular process while watching on video to confirm the vocal process itself moves medially and down, not just the whole supraglottis.
Place the suture
Pass a double-armed 4-0 monofilament suture through the muscular process twice in a figure-of-eight to get secure purchase.
Route the suture anteriorly

Bring both arms through the paraglottic plane to the window without catching tissue that would alter the pull vector. Pass one through the cartilage in front of the window (drill if calcified) and the other under the inferior strut out through the cricothyroid membrane.
Test the vector
Clamp the arms and pull gently forward while the patient counts, judging voice and endoscopic closure, together with depth gauge testing of the medialization.
Place the implant
Insert the Silastic or Gore-Tex implant with the adduction suture lying deep to it, sizing the implant before edema accumulates.
Tie with light tension
Adjust tension while listening and watching and tie over the anterior thyroid cartilage; only light tension is needed, as over-rotation worsens the voice.
Close and observe

Close straps and skin with a small drain at discretion. Admit overnight with IV steroids because edema and airway compromise are more likely than with medialization alone; check for a piriform tear with irrigation and Valsalva before closing.

steps: Indications

Standard treatment for adductor laryngeal dystonia (TA-LCA) and abductor dystonia (posterior cricoarytenoid); also used for vocal tremor, refractory granuloma, temporizing bilateral paralysis (about 2.5 U per side), and refractory cough.
Contraindications

Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding, neuromuscular junction disease such as myasthenia gravis, and with concurrent aminoglycosides; impaired abduction is a relative contraindication to posterior cricoarytenoid injection.
Prepare the toxin

Reconstitute a 100-U vial with preservative-free saline to the chosen concentration and keep the volume small (ideally 0.1 mL per fold) to limit diffusion; draw up with a larger needle, then attach an insulated 26–27 gauge EMG needle.
Dose

Start adductor patients at a low-average dose (about 1 U per side) and adjust by detailed patient diaries; there is no standard dose. For abductor dystonia, inject one posterior cricoarytenoid (about 5–7.5 U) and reassess at 2 weeks before treating the other.
Position and ground
Seat the patient semi-reclined with the neck extended (shoulder roll if the neck is short), attach ground and reference electrodes, and ask the patient to breathe quietly and not swallow.
EMG-guided TA-LCA entry

Bend the needle up 30–45 degrees (more in women), enter the cricothyroid membrane 2–3 mm off midline, and advance superiorly and laterally, staying submucosal; a hollow airway sound means you are in the lumen and should redirect laterally.
Confirm and inject
Inject when phonation produces brisk recruitment and a full interference pattern, ideally with a prephonatory burst. Repeat on the other side with equal dosing, staged or simultaneous per practice.
Posterior cricoarytenoid injection

Rotate the larynx with the thumb on the posterior thyroid border and enter behind it toward the cricoid lamina, or go through the cricothyroid membrane across the airway and through the cricoid. Confirm activation with sniffing before injecting.
Endoscope-guided percutaneous option

With 4% lidocaine instilled transtracheally and a flexible scope on a monitor, pass a 27-gauge needle through the cricothyroid membrane into the subglottis and into the posterior third of the membranous fold. This is easier to learn, but needs higher doses, starts up to 5 days later, and is less consistent.
Supraglottic per-oral option

After nasal, oral, and laryngeal topical anesthesia, guide a curved 27-gauge injector into the posterolateral or mid false fold and raise a superficial submucosal bleb. Use about 5–7.5 U per side (2.5 U per 0.1 mL); deeper injection causes breathiness.
Weigh the supraglottic tradeoff

Supraglottic injection smooths the peaks and troughs and causes little breathiness, which suits professional voice users and supraglottic tremor, but lasts only about 8–10 weeks and is technically harder.
Counsel on the effect

Expect several days of marked weakness (breathiness, liquid dysphagia) followed by a 3–4 month plateau of therapeutic effect; dyspnea and stridor are the early risk after posterior cricoarytenoid injection.
Aftercare
Discharge immediately with no voice restriction. Keep the patient NPO for 60–90 minutes if the larynx was anesthetized, and give a written handout on side effects and when to seek care.

steps: Plan from the exam

Choose the technique from endoscopy and anterior rhinoscopy: caudal deformity, diffuse deviation, posterior deflection, or an isolated spur. Note prior septal surgery. CT is optional; it helps with posterior deflections and concha bullosa but can misrepresent how deviated the septum looks on exam.
Decongest and infiltrate

Apply topical decongestant pledgets, then inject 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine into the septal mucosa on both sides, hydrodissecting the subperichondrial plane. Wait about 15 minutes for full vasoconstriction before incising.
Make the incision

Retract the columella to the opposite side and make a hemitransfixion incision along the caudal septal edge from the anterior to the posterior septal angle with a 15 blade. Use a Killian incision instead when only posterior work is needed.
Find the correct plane

Incise the perichondrium at the caudal edge and elevate in the subperichondrial plane, where bare cartilage looks pearly white and feels gritty. A bloodless field and an intact flap confirm the right layer.
Cross the bony-cartilaginous junction

Where cartilage meets bone, perichondrium and periosteum do not join and dense fibers sit between them; divide these sharply and continue subperiosteally over the perpendicular plate, vomer, and crest to cover every area of deflection.
Elevate the opposite side

Raise a contralateral flap from the caudal edge, or through a chondrotomy just anterior to the deflection if a Killian incision was used. Avoid tears that face each other on both sides, the main cause of perforation.
Resect deviated cartilage

Excise the deflected quadrangular cartilage while keeping an L-strut of at least 15 mm dorsally and caudally to support the dorsum and tip. Straighten or morselize some cartilage for replacement into the pocket if needed.
Remove bony deflections

Take deviated perpendicular plate and vomer with a double-action rongeur or through-cutting instrument, never by twisting, which can fracture the cribriform region and cause a CSF leak. Use a chisel for a prominent maxillary crest.
Correct caudal deviation

Score the concave side along the bend to release memory. For a swinging door, free the cartilage from the crest groove, trim an inferior strip, swing it to midline, and fix it to the nasal spine periosteum with a figure-of-eight absorbable suture; or use the doorstop variant.
Endoscopic septoplasty for posterior deviation

After an initial pocket under headlight, continue elevation with a 0-degree scope and suction Freer past the junction, make a septotomy in front of the worst deviation, elevate the opposite side, and resect the bent segment; posterior bone does not need to be preserved.
Directed approach for an isolated spur
Endoscopically make a horizontal incision directly over the spur apex, raise flaps above and below, remove the spur with a through-cutter or microdebrider, then simply lay the flaps back in place.
Severe caudal deformity options

When the caudal septum is badly bent, buttress it with a perpendicular plate (ethmoid) bone graft, or use an open approach with extracorporeal septoplasty, rebuilding an L-strut outside the nose; PDS foil can supplement weak cartilage.
Close the pocket

Prevent hematoma with a running absorbable quilting stitch (for example 4-0 plain gut on a straight needle), with or without silicone splints. If no tear exists, a small floor incision lets blood drain. Close the incision in one layer.
Postoperative care
Packing is rarely needed. Remove splints at 2 to 7 days. Counsel about hematoma, perforation, and dorsal or tip change from strut loss, and reassess airflow rather than cosmetic straightness.

steps: Confirm the target

Treat turbinate obstruction only after rhinitis therapy and after separating fixed hypertrophy from valve or septal causes. Remember the anterior 2 cm of the inferior turbinate drives most of its airflow effect.
Choose the least invasive option

Escalate from outfracture to submucosal soft-tissue reduction to submucosal bone plus soft tissue to anterior full-thickness resection. Total turbinectomy is for tumor only because over-resection risks empty nose syndrome.
Inject
Inject 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine into the anterior inferior turbinate (or middle turbinate insertion) under endoscopic view to limit bleeding.
Outfracture correctly

Place a Freer in the inferior meatus and infracture the turbinate up and medially, then push it inferolaterally from its superomedial surface. Work gently near the inferior meatus to protect the nasolacrimal opening. Outfracture alone does not treat vascular hypertrophy.
Enter the submucosa
For microdebrider reduction, make a stab incision just behind the mucocutaneous junction of the turbinate head and elevate a subperiosteal pocket off the bone.
Sculpt soft tissue

Insert the turbinate blade into the pocket, window facing away from the bone and the surface mucosa, and sweep at slow oscillation through the anterior two-thirds until adequately reduced. Cauterize the stab incision if it bleeds.
Energy-device alternatives

For radiofrequency or cautery, follow device settings, insert the probe into the anterior turbinate, and make several passes deep to the surface to avoid sloughing and crusting. Radiofrequency is mucosa-sparing; laser and needle cautery are less precise.
Remove hypertrophic bone

If the conchal bone is bulky, extend the pocket and take the anterior half to two-thirds of the bone with Blakesley forceps using a twisting motion, the scope placed under the flap for view, then complete soft-tissue reduction.
Anterior partial resection when needed

For severe disease, infracture, remove lateral soft tissue and anterior lateral bone with through-cutters and backbiters, and resect only the anterior 1–2 cm; redrape mucosa. Expect longer crusting where bone is exposed.
Avoid the posterior turbinate
Posterior work adds little airway benefit and risks brisk bleeding from sphenopalatine branches entering the tail; keep reduction anterior.
Open a concha bullosa

Inject the middle turbinate, incise its anterior face vertically into the air cell, spread with scissors, extend the cut back to the basal lamella, and free the lateral lamella. Keep the medial wall, which ties toward the cribriform plate; do not just crush it.
Manage the middle turbinate carefully

If partial middle turbinectomy is needed, block the SPA, cut the superior and posterior attachments with scissors, remove only the lower half, and cauterize the posterior stump. Avoid avulsion from the skull base (CSF leak, smell loss).
Prevent lateralization

Preserve the inferior basal lamella, then medialize with a controlled scar to the septum (pack 5–7 days) or an absorbable transseptal suture. Consider endoscopic septoplasty instead of turbinate resection to open the middle meatus.
Aftercare
Most cases are outpatient with acetaminophen and saline. Debride crusts and synechiae at follow-up; pack only after aggressive procedures to hold mucosal flaps.
inferior-turbinate-reduction.source_label: the Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery, 2e, Ch 2, pp 11–18

steps: Select the patient

Offer early SPA ligation for posterior epistaxis that fails packing, since early surgery shortens stay and cost. It is not designed for anticoagulant-driven oozing or for HHT. Ask about supplements and look for tumor red flags such as diplopia or numbness.
Prepare
Use general anesthesia to protect the airway. Consent for possible anterior ethmoid artery ligation. CT is optional but helps navigation when anatomy is unusual.
Control the field

Place oxymetazoline pledgets, inject transnasally near the foramen, and consider a transoral greater palatine canal injection of lidocaine with epinephrine. Hot water irrigation at about 50°C or bipolar can slow mucosal bleeding.
Create working room
Medialize the middle turbinate and pledget the middle meatus. Remove a large uncinate if it limits access; a maxillary antrostomy adds the posterior antral wall as a landmark.
Incise the lateral wall

Find where the middle turbinate basal lamella attaches to the palatine bone and make a vertical mucoperiosteal incision about 1 cm anterior to it, palpating the junction of the antrum and palatine bone with a ball probe.
Raise the flap
Elevate the mucoperiosteum posteriorly with a Cottle or suction Freer, sweeping from inferior to superior, staying on bone.
Identify the crista ethmoidalis

Find the small bony crest of the palatine bone; the SPA emerges just behind or behind-and-above it, within about 1 mm in most people. If lost, follow the middle turbinate attachment, which the SPA supplies.
Remove the crista
Take down the crista and bone over the foramen with a 1-mm Kerrison to expose the trunk before it branches, which is associated with fewer rebleeds.
Dissect all branches

Free the pedicle circumferentially with a ball probe and look for every branch: most people have two or more and two-thirds have three or more, and some branch before the foramen through separate openings.
Clip and cauterize
Place hemoclips on the trunk and each branch and bipolar the branches distally, or use bipolar alone. Missing a branch is the commonest cause of failure.
Close

Lay the flap back over the palatine bone and place an absorbable spacer in the middle meatus to hold the flap and keep the turbinate medial. Place resorbable dressings where prior packing traumatized mucosa.
Recovery and failure
Observe roughly 12 hours before discharge. If bleeding continues, suspect a missed SPA branch or anterior ethmoid territory and consider AEA ligation.

steps: Read the CT

Note the uncinate's relation to the lamina (a lateralized, atelectatic uncinate puts the orbit at risk), Haller cells, concha bullosa, and disease on the floor or anterior wall that will need angled scopes and instruments.
Use the induction window
Blood pressure and heart rate peak in the first 15 minutes after induction; use that time for decongestion. Place pledgets high to shrink the septal swell body and wait at least 5 minutes.
Inject
Inject about 1 mL of lidocaine with epinephrine at the middle turbinate axilla and 1 mL into its anterior head, watching the mucosa blanch, to keep the lateral turbinate from bleeding.
Make space

Gently medialize the middle turbinate with a Freer and pledget the meatus; a relaxing cut at the basal lamella corner can help. Outfracture the inferior turbinate and correct a blocking septal deviation.
Identify landmarks
With a 0-degree scope find the uncinate free edge, the agger nasi bulge, and the inferior turbinate insertion. The maxillary line marks the uncinate attachment to the lacrimal bone.
Reflect the uncinate
Use a ball probe to flip the free edge of the uncinate forward and open the infundibulum.
Backbite the uncinate

Open the backbiter at 12 o'clock, pronate behind the free edge, and bite posterior to anterior until the firm lacrimal bone is felt: bite to the hard bone, not through it. Avoid sickle knife incisions over an atelectatic uncinate.
Remove superior and inferior remnants
Take the upper uncinate with 45- or 90-degree through-cutters or an angled debrider (short taps), and the lower part down to the inferior turbinate with a downbiter.
Find the natural ostium
Switch to a 30-degree scope; the ostium lies behind the maxillary line at the junction of its lower third and upper two-thirds, near the height of the lower third of the middle turbinate.
Enlarge to fit the disease

For recurrent acute disease, enlarge the ostium minimally. For polyps, hyperplastic mucosa, or revision, extend posteriorly through the fontanelle with a straight through-cutter toward the palatine bone, always incorporating the natural ostium.
Clear the sinus
With 45- or 70-degree scopes, remove polyps with angled debriders and flush out all allergic mucin; use giraffe forceps for retention cysts and Haller cells on the floor or anterior wall.
Final check
Look again with an angled scope and palpate the lacrimal bone with a probe to confirm no uncinate remains, which prevents recirculation.
Prevent scarring
Medialize the middle turbinate by suture or controlled scarring to stop synechiae to the lateral wall, and plan debridement visits.

steps: Define the extent

Partial ethmoidectomy (bulla and cells anterior to the basal lamella, a mini-FESS with antrostomy) suits recurrent acute or nonpolypoid disease; complete ethmoidectomy to the sphenoid is for polyps, revision, or posterior disease.
Study the CT

Count ethmoid cells above the maxillary sinus roof, judge skull base slope on sagittal views, note a tall maxillary sinus with a short ethmoid roof (higher skull base risk), Onodi cells, lateral lamella length, and AEA position.
Block the pterygopalatine vessels

Inject 1–2 mL of lidocaine with epinephrine transnasally about 1 cm above the inferior edge of the middle turbinate attachment, or into the greater palatine canal medial to the second molar with a bent needle after aspirating.
Open the bulla
After the antrostomy, medialize the turbinate with a J-curette, enter the retrobullar space medial and behind the bulla, and fracture the bulla forward and laterally.
Clear the anterior ethmoid

Remove fragments and take lateral bulla partitions off the lamina with Kerrison punches and angled through-cutters. Avoid making raw surfaces on the posterior agger nasi and superior bulla at the same level.
Set the height
Keep the maxillary sinus roof in view as the height limit while moving posteriorly; it keeps you low where the skull base descends.
Enter the basal lamella
Perforate the inferomedial basal lamella with a J-curette at the height of the maxillary roof, near the junction of its vertical and horizontal segments. Entering too high leads into the skull base.
Open the posterior ethmoid
Remove the vertical basal lamella down to the horizontal segment and up to roof height with debrider and through-cutters, but preserve the horizontal segment to keep the turbinate stable.
Reach the sphenoid face
Clear posterior cells to the sphenoid face, using the superior turbinate as a guide. Do not mistake an Onodi cell's posterior wall for the sphenoid face; the optic nerve runs in its roof.
Find the skull base posteriorly
Identify the skull base at the sphenoid or posterior ethmoid roof, then switch to a 30-degree (reverse-post) scope.
Clear the skull base back to front

Remove partitions from posterior to anterior with upbiting through-cutters, cutting only when you can see in front of a partition and feel behind it. Use the microdebrider only for mucosa, never for bone on the skull base or lamina.
Stop at the bulla roof
Continue forward to the bulla roof and suprabullar recess, which marks the AEA and the start of the frontal recess dissection.
Stay oriented and hemostatic
Zoom out in front of the turbinate periodically. Control bleeding at the inferior basal lamella (SPA branches) with suction cautery, and never strip skull base or orbital mucosa.
Finish
Medialize the middle turbinate by suture or controlled scarring and arrange early debridements to prevent lateralization and synechiae.

steps: Pick the route
Use the transnasal route medial to the middle turbinate for isolated sphenoid disease or pituitary access; use the transethmoid route as part of complete FESS.
Review CT

Note pneumatization, Onodi cells, optic and carotid dehiscence, the intersinus septum's posterior attachment (often the carotid canal), thickened osteitic bone from fungal balls, and the height of the sphenopalatine foramen to predict the septal artery.
Block bleeding
Inject the greater palatine canal (needle bent 1.5–2 cm at 45 degrees, aspirate, 1–2 mL) or transnasally above the middle turbinate attachment, and pledget the sphenoethmoid recess.
Expose the recess

With a 0-degree scope, lateralize the middle turbinate (transnasal) or complete the posterior ethmoidectomy to see the superior turbinate and its lamellae (transethmoid). Removing superior ethmoid cells improves light.
Trim the superior turbinate
Excise the lower half of the superior turbinate with a straight through-cutter; the natural ostium sits medial and posterior to it. Spare the upper part, which carries olfactory fibers.
Enter the ostium
Pass a J-curette into the natural ostium, low and medial, and fracture the sphenoid face laterally. Work from known to unknown.
Use the Bolger box if needed
Without a usable superior turbinate, outline a box bounded by the superior turbinate, its basal lamella, the ethmoid roof, and the orbit, and enter medial and inferior to its diagonal.
Enlarge
Widen with Kerrison or straight mushroom punches; use a drill if the face is thick from osteitis.
Respect the septal artery
When opening inferiorly, expect the posterior septal branch running horizontally across the lower face; cauterize it or stay above it, especially if a nasoseptal flap may be needed later.
Handle an Onodi cell
An Onodi cell sits above the true ostium; never go through its posterior wall. After finding the sphenoid low and medial, take down the Onodi floor to merge the cavities.
Clear the sinus

Inspect lateral and inferior recesses with 30- to 70-degree scopes and remove fungal debris or pus with suction and irrigation; do not engage a microdebrider inside the sinus or twist a septum attached to the carotid.
Protect mucosa
Avoid stripping mucosa on the skull base or lamina, which leads to edema and neo-osteogenesis, and follow with debridement to keep the opening patent.

steps: Indications

Use IIb for failed IIa from neo-osteogenesis, a lateralized turbinate remnant, or a prominent beak; mucoceles; reopening an obliterated sinus; type 3/4 or septal cells; tumors; CSF leak; selected fractures. Avoid with very narrow A-P diameter or severe bilateral neo-osteogenesis.
Plan on CT and MRI

Check that the drill fits without its back end hitting the cribriform plate or posterior table (often quoted 10 mm), beak thickness, olfactory fossa projection, turbinate remnant, AEA (cauterize early if on a mesentery), and posterior table dehiscence. MRI separates tumor from secretions.
Set up

Tape the tube to the lower left lip, use TIVA and 15–20 degrees reverse Trendelenburg, apply strong topical vasoconstrictor, and inject the middle turbinate, lateral wall, and septum. Have navigation, angled drills, and CSF repair materials ready.
Complete the IIa first
Perform at least an anterior ethmoidectomy to see the lamina and finish the frontal recess dissection as in a IIa.
Define the AEA

Identify the AEA as the posterior boundary on that side and follow the skull base forward, opening supraorbital cells into the recess. If neo-osteogenesis hides everything, stop and work from the other side.
Trace the floor
Picture the horseshoe-shaped frontal floor and confirm with navigation. Use a minitrephine with fluorescein irrigation if the outflow cannot be found.
Resect the anterior middle turbinate
Make a scissor cut just below the turbinate's anterior skull base attachment toward the AEA level and a second cut from below to meet it; refine with through-cutters and keep the lower turbinate.
Punch the floor
Remove the frontal floor anteriorly and medially with 45-degree mushroom, Hosemann, or Bachert punches, as far as bone thickness allows.
Drill to enlarge
Use a 70-degree diamond drill, thinning the beak anteriorly first, then medially, alternating with punches; use cutting burs for a thick beak only after the sinus and skull base are seen.
Watch the bur's back
Keep track of the posterior surface of the drill to avoid skull base penetration, and avoid unnecessary mucosal removal.
Clean and optimize
Remove pus, bone chips, and dust; cauterize the cut edges of turbinate and septum; consider a thin pliable silicone stent with a defined duration.
Rescue variant
For a lateralized turbinate remnant, raise a medially based mucosal flap off the remnant before removing it and advance it over bare bone after the IIb (frontal sinus rescue).
Aftercare
Tapered oral steroids, culture-directed antibiotics if infected, early saline, topical steroid drops with head positioning, and weekly debridement until stable; the neo-ostium matures for a year.

draf.title: Frontal Sinusotomy — Draf IIb (Extended Unilateral)

steps: Optimize first
Treat inflammation medically before revision; a preoperative oral steroid course reduces difficulty and blood loss in polyp cases. Plan a frontal recess dissection too, aiming for a last operation.
Map dangers on CT

Use 2–3 mm or thinner CT with reformats. Note orbital and skull base dehiscence, lateral lamella depth, AEA course, Onodi cells, a lateralized turbinate remnant, and residual osteitic partitions along the lamina and skull base.
Check the 2:1 ratio
If maxillary sinus height is more than twice the posterior ethmoid height, a trajectory taken from the maxillary sinus will head into the skull base instead of the sphenoid.
Check carotid and septum
Carotid dehiscence in the sphenoid occurs in about 5–25%; with asymmetric sphenoids the intersinus septum usually inserts on one carotid canal, so it must not be twisted.
Decongest
Use topical oxymetazoline, 4% cocaine, or 1:1000 adrenaline pledgets plus local injection to control an inflamed, bloody field.
Debulk polyps
Clear nasal and middle meatal polyps with the microdebrider, removing only soft tissue; leave bone work to hand instruments for better tactile feedback.
Revise the antrostomy

Remove the uncinate remnant back to the lacrimal bone with a backbiter, connect any scarred natural ostium to prevent recirculation, and flush polyps and mucin with a syringe on a curved olive-tip suction.
Remove the air scoop
Take the posterior fontanelle and osteitic posterior medial maxillary wall back flush with the posterior antral wall using straight through-cutters.
Skeletonize the lamina
Remove osteitic partitions from the medial orbital wall with 2- and 4-mm Kerrison punches and 45-degree through-cutters, following the curve of the orbital floor up onto the medial wall.
Reach the sphenoid
Clear the remaining posterior ethmoid cells; the last cell is pyramid-shaped, and the posterior maxillary wall curving back approximates the sphenoid face.
Enlarge the sphenoidotomy

Open from the natural os laterally and inferiorly with Kerrison or mushroom punches; retract the inferior mucosa with a Freer to protect the septal branch of the SPA while removing bone, then clear mucin from the sphenoid floor.
Clear the skull base

Identify the skull base in the sphenoid and work posterior to anterior, erring laterally against the lamina; debride polyps with a 40-degree blade and cut partitions only when you can see in front and feel behind.
Remove the superior uncinate
Finish anteriorly by removing the superior uncinate remnant along the anteromedial orbital wall and complete frontal recess work as needed.
Close and counsel
Packing is usually unnecessary (most patients need none); a middle meatal spacer reduces synechiae. No nose blowing, to limit bleeding and orbital emphysema.

steps: Confirm and image
Confirm CSF with beta-2 transferrin. Obtain thin-cut CT for the bony defect, Keros depth, and asymmetry, and MRI if a soft tissue mass suggests meningoencephalocele.
Intrathecal fluorescein
If used, give 0.1 mL of 10% fluorescein diluted in 10 mL of CSF or saline slowly via lumbar puncture or drain, with consent for off-label use; a blue-light filter shows low-flow leaks.
Anesthesia setup
Use TIVA with head up 10–15 degrees and agree a deep, smooth extubation with no bag-mask ventilation to avoid pneumocephalus.
Plan the flap early
If a nasoseptal flap may be needed, raise it before any inferior sphenoidotomy or posterior septectomy and store it in the nasopharynx or maxillary sinus.
Harvest the flap

Cut along the choanal arch and vomer, along the floor, superiorly from the sphenoid os while sparing 1–2 cm of olfactory mucosa, and anteriorly as far as needed; elevate subperichondrially, from the floor upward at the nasal spine.
Expose the defect
Complete antrostomy, sphenoethmoidectomy, and frontal sinusotomy as needed; resect the middle turbinate to see the cribriform plate and lateral lamella, saving its mucosa and bone for grafts.
Reduce the encephalocele
Circumferentially expose the sac and shrink it to the bony edge with bipolar or coblation, controlling vessels that could retract intracranially.
Prepare the bed
Strip mucosa around the defect, remove char, and measure the defect so no functional mucosa is trapped beneath grafts.
Choose the repair

Small (under about 5 mm), low-flow, no encephalocele: free mucosal graft or flap. Larger or with encephalocele: add a rigid bone or composite underlay. Large (over 2–3 cm) or high-flow defects: subdural inlay plus vascularized flap.
Place the layers
Tuck a dural substitute or fascia inlay under the bony edges, then lay the flap or free graft mucosal side facing the nose (ink free grafts) over the center and dependent edges without gaps.
Test and bolster
Check with Valsalva, then add sealant, a frontal stent if swelling could block the frontal sinus, Gelfoam, and removable packing or a Foley balloon that supports packing without pushing grafts.
Postoperative care

Neuro checks, consider head CT, packs at least 5 days, no straining or nose blowing; lumbar drain only selectively (10–15 mL/h for 2–5 days); long-term acetazolamide and pressure workup for spontaneous leaks.

steps: Time-out and positioning

Confirm the side, the indication, the planned tube type and whether adenoidectomy is added. With the child supine under mask anesthesia, turn the head away from the operative ear and bring in the binocular operating microscope. Choose the largest ear speculum that fits the canal comfortably so you get a wide view without lacerating the canal skin.
Clear the canal

Under magnification, remove cerumen and debris with a curette, loop or fine suction, working along the canal floor and avoiding the thin skin over the bony canal. Bleeding canal skin hides the drum and the tube site, so take your time. If the canal is too narrow or stenotic, a smaller speculum is safer than forcing a larger one.
Inspect the whole drum

Before cutting, look at the entire tympanic membrane: annulus, malleus handle, umbo, pars flaccida and the posterosuperior quadrant. Look for a retraction pocket, cholesteatoma, perforation or a vascular mass behind the drum. A bluish or red mass inferiorly suggests a high jugular bulb or an aberrant carotid. If you find one, change the incision site or stop.
Choose the incision site

The standard site is the anteroinferior quadrant of the pars tensa, away from the ossicles and the posterosuperior quadrant, where the incus and stapes sit. Stay a couple of millimetres in from the annulus. If the anterior canal wall bulges and blocks that view, use an inferior or anterosuperior site, but never the posterosuperior quadrant.
Make the myringotomy

Make a short radial cut with the myringotomy knife, using only enough depth to go through the drum. Do not push the blade into the middle ear, where it can hit the promontory or a dehiscent jugular bulb. Make the cut just large enough for the tube. If it is too big, the tube may come out early.
Aspirate the effusion

Suction the middle-ear fluid through the incision with a fine suction tip, without passing the tip deep into the middle ear. Record whether the fluid is serous, mucoid or purulent. If thick glue will not clear, a small counterincision in the inferior drum or saline irrigation through the myringotomy helps you aspirate it. A dry ear is a finding too. Record it.
Load the tube

Hold the short-term tube by its outer flange in alligator forceps, with the inner flange pointing toward the drum. Keep the tube's long axis lined up with the incision. Have a Rosen needle or pick ready to guide it. Choose a long-term (T-type) tube only for a planned need for long ventilation, and counsel the family about the higher rate of a lasting hole after it comes out.
Insert the inner flange

Tuck the leading edge of the inner flange through one end of the incision. Then push or rotate the rest through with the needle or pick so the inner flange sits medial to the drum. Do not push the whole tube through the hole. If a tube falls into the middle ear, retrieve it under magnification if you can do so easily; do not chase it blindly.
Seat and check the tube

Check that the drum is pinched between the two flanges, with the shaft at right angles to the drum and the lumen open toward the canal. A tube lying in the canal skin, or buried under the drum or in the middle-ear mucosa, needs to be repositioned. Gently suction blood or mucus out of the lumen without pulling the tube out.
Manage bleeding and debris

Stop canal or drum bleeding with gentle pressure or a cotton pledget soaked in a vasoconstrictor. Do not suction hard over the tube, which can pull it out. Remove blood clot from the canal so the tube can be judged at follow-up. Record any canal tear or unusual drum finding.
Repeat on the other ear

Reposition the head and repeat the whole sequence on the second ear: clear the canal, inspect the drum, pick the site, cut, aspirate, insert and check. Judge that ear on its own findings. A wall that bulges, a retraction or a vascular mass on the second side may change the site or the plan.
Final check and handoff

Look again at both tubes for position, an open lumen and bleeding before the child wakes. Record the effusion type, the tube type and side, and any adenoidectomy. Arrange the first ear check. Give the family return signs: drainage that lasts after a course of drops, bleeding, or pain.

steps: Team brief and equipment check

Agree with anesthesia on the question the scope must answer, spontaneous versus controlled ventilation, and the rescue plan. Lay out the laryngoscopes, Hopkins rod telescopes (0 and 30 degree), ventilating bronchoscopes, the age-appropriate endotracheal tube, and at least one size smaller tube and scope. Have a probe and suction ready. Apply antifog to the lenses just before use.
Induction and topical anesthesia

Inhalational or intravenous induction is chosen to match the airway. Most units keep spontaneous breathing, which shows dynamic collapse and vocal-fold movement. Measure topical lidocaine to the larynx and trachea by weight, because adult preparations easily overdose infants. Be ready for laryngospasm after spraying, and give dexamethasone at induction if you suspect stenosis or plan instrumentation.
Position and protect

Place a small roll under the shoulders without hyperextending the neck. Support the head of a small infant. Protect the lips, gums and teeth with a guard or moist gauze. Use a Mayo stand or flexible arm to hold the suspension laryngoscope so the premaxilla and chest take no pressure.
Expose the larynx

Pass the lubricated laryngoscope down the midline with the tongue centered. Look at the oropharynx, tongue base, vallecula and supraglottis as you advance. Lift the epiglottis to expose the glottis without forcing. If you meet resistance or the view is poor, stop and reposition. Forcing the blade injures teeth and lips and swells the airway.
Examine the supraglottis and glottis

With the telescope, record the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids and vocal folds. Use a probe to move each arytenoid and test cricoarytenoid joint mobility. Pass the probe between the arytenoids to exclude a posterior laryngeal cleft. Watch vocal-fold movement as anesthesia lightens, with anesthesia calling the phase of breathing.
Inspect the subglottis

Gently part the vocal folds or pass a thin telescope through the glottis to view the subglottis all the way around. Record scar, edema, cysts, a hemangioma, or a narrow, elliptical cricoid. If stenosis is significant, an ultrathin telescope through the laryngoscope causes less trauma than a bronchoscope. Note the distance from the vocal folds to the top and bottom of any narrowing.
Tracheobronchoscopy

Advance the telescope or ventilating bronchoscope through the trachea to the carina, keeping the membranous wall posterior to stay oriented. Inspect both mainstem bronchi and their openings. Look for tracheomalacia with a small scope pulled back and no positive pressure, so the airway is not splinted open. Record pulsatile compression, complete rings, a tracheoesophageal fistula or a foreign body.
Size any stenosis

When it changes management, size the narrowing with graduated endotracheal tubes and record the outer diameter and the tube brand. Find the largest tube that leaks at about 10 to 25 cm H2O, and give the Myer-Cotton grade from a validated chart. Never force a tube or scope through resistance. If a lesion cannot be passed safely, record that and change the plan.
Dynamic assessment on emergence

As the child lightens, pull the scope back to just behind the epiglottis tip, or use a 30 or 70 degree telescope. Look for supraglottic collapse, vocal-fold paralysis and paradoxical movement. Have anesthesia call inspiration and expiration. Gentle suction at the laryngeal inlet can mimic the inspiratory collapse of laryngomalacia.
Perform planned interventions

Only after the whole airway is recorded, carry out planned biopsy, cyst removal, scar incision, balloon dilation, granulation removal or foreign-body extraction. Before each step, confirm with anesthesia that oxygen levels are stable. If saturation falls, stop, take out instruments that block the airway, let anesthesia re-oxygenate, and then decide whether to go on.
Reinspect the treated airway

Pass the telescope again through the full airway. Check for bleeding, mucosal tears, loose tissue, edema, and how much lumen was gained. Control oozing with pledgets soaked in topical vasoconstrictor. Take photographs or video of the key findings and the result so later scopes can be compared.
Airway disposition

Decide with anesthesia whether to extubate in the OR, keep the child intubated (with tube size and position recorded), or monitor in the ICU. Record the grade, lesion level and length, vocal-fold movement, any second lesion, steroid plans, and the rescue plan. Tell recovery staff about the plan for stridor after extubation.

steps: Team brief

Agree with anesthesia on spontaneous ventilation without a tube, measured topical lidocaine and dexamethasone at induction. If a CO2 laser is used, plan laser safety: low inspired oxygen, wet eye pads and wet pledgets. Have microscissors, cupped forceps, the laser or a laryngeal microdebrider, and pledgets soaked in topical vasoconstrictor ready. Have a smaller endotracheal tube ready to rescue the airway.
Diagnostic laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy

Start with full airway endoscopy to confirm the collapse pattern and exclude a second lesion such as subglottic stenosis, tracheomalacia, vocal-fold paralysis or a laryngeal cleft. These are found in up to about a quarter of children. Probe between the arytenoids for a cleft. A distal lesion may change the plan, or may be the real cause of symptoms.
Suspend the larynx

Suspend with a Parsons, Benjamin or Lindholm laryngoscope placed in the vallecula. This keeps the epiglottis and both aryepiglottic folds in view with room for two hands. Protect the gums and lips. Bring in the microscope with a 400 mm lens, or use a telescope with video. Anesthesia gives the anesthetic through a side port or a catheter in the nasopharynx.
Define the collapse pattern

Under magnification, find the short aryepiglottic folds, redundant cuneiform and arytenoid mucosa, an omega-shaped or backward-falling epiglottis, and the interarytenoid mucosa. Identify the true vocal folds as the lower boundary. Gentle suction at the inlet shows which tissue falls in on breathing in. The shape of the collapse decides how much you cut.
Divide the aryepiglottic fold

Grasp the fold and divide the short aryepiglottic fold with microscissors or the laser. Cut close to the lateral edge of the epiglottis, aiming toward the depth of the vallecula. This lets the epiglottis spring forward. Keep the cut shallow and in front of the arytenoid. Do not cut into the pharyngoepiglottic fold or the lateral pharyngeal wall.
Trim redundant arytenoid mucosa

Grasp the prolapsing mucosa over the cuneiform cartilage and the lateral arytenoid, and trim it conservatively with scissors, laser or microdebrider. Stay lateral and above the arytenoid apex. Keep the mucosa between the arytenoids and over the inner surfaces of the arytenoids. Removing tissue there causes supraglottic or posterior glottic stenosis.
Treat the opposite side

Repeat the release on the other side only as far as that side's collapse needs, keeping it symmetric and leaving mucosa intact between the raw areas. Some surgeons do one side first in children with neurologic disease or a high risk of aspiration. Be cautious in syndromes such as CHARGE, where surgery can make the epiglottis collapse more.
Address the epiglottis if needed

If the epiglottis still falls backward and blocks the airway, consider an epiglottopexy. Remove mucosa from the tongue surface of the epiglottis and the matching tongue base, then suture the epiglottis forward. For a tightly curled epiglottis, a single cut on one side of it can unfurl it. Never cut both sides, which risks stenosis.
Hemostasis

Control oozing with pledgets soaked in topical vasoconstrictor and pinpoint suction cautery or laser, using as little heat as possible. Remove all pledgets and count them. Check the vocal folds and subglottis for laser or mechanical injury and for blood in the trachea, and suction any blood.
Reassess the airway

With the child breathing on their own, compare the supraglottic opening with the starting view. The folds should no longer fall in on breathing in. Take photographs. If the airway still collapses, consider whether more conservative trimming now, or a later revision, is safer than taking more tissue today.
Emergence and disposition

Most infants can be extubated in the OR. Decide on overnight intubation or ICU monitoring for severe sleep apnea, neurologic or heart and lung disease, very young age, or extensive surgery. Avoid a nasogastric tube when possible to limit swelling. Record the feeding plan and a check of swallowing.
Postoperative checks

Plan for stridor, breathing effort, oxygen needs and feeding to be checked as anesthesia wears off, with clear triggers to call. If swallowing problems were present before surgery, plan a swallow check. Arrange a clinic visit to follow weight gain and symptoms, and repeat endoscopy if stridor or poor growth persists.

steps: Baseline exam and forced ductions

After induction, place corneal shields and repeat forced ductions. Grasp the inferior rectus insertion through the conjunctiva in the inferior fornix with fine-toothed forceps and rotate the globe up and down. Compare with the other eye. Record the pupils, globe position and the CT defect so the result can be judged against this baseline at the end.
Lid traction and globe protection

Place a 4-0 silk traction suture through the gray line of the lower lid. Protect the cornea with a Jaeger plate or a malleable retractor. Inject local anesthetic with epinephrine into the lower-lid conjunctiva. For better exposure, plan a lateral canthotomy with release of the inferior limb of the canthal tendon.
Transconjunctival incision

With a needle-tip cautery, incise the conjunctiva and lower-lid retractors below the tarsus. Run from just lateral to the punctum and caruncle to the lateral canthus, staying clear of the canaliculus. Put a traction suture through the conjunctival edge and pull it up over the cornea to protect the globe. A subciliary approach is an alternative but has a higher risk of ectropion.
Preseptal dissection to the rim

Dissect in the preseptal plane, between the orbicularis and the orbital septum, down to the infraorbital rim. Keep the septum intact so fat does not bulge into the field. Use a Desmarres retractor on the lid and a malleable retractor on the orbit. Expose the arcus marginalis along the rim from the medial to the lateral side.
Incise and elevate periosteum

Incise the periosteum just in front of the arcus marginalis on the front face of the rim. This keeps the septum and leaves a cuff for closure. Lift the periorbita over the rim and onto the orbital floor with a Freer or periosteal elevator. Stay in the subperiosteal plane, and protect the infraorbital nerve as it leaves its foramen below the rim.
Define the defect edges

Raise the periorbita backward around the whole fracture, using a Freer in one hand and suction in the other while malleable retractors gently hold back the orbit. Find intact bone on every side: the medial edge at the inferomedial strut, the lateral edge at the inferior orbital fissure, and especially the stable posterior ledge. Do not extend dissection toward the apex.
Reduce herniated tissue

Ease herniated fat, periorbita and any trapped inferior rectus out of the maxillary sinus, working hand over hand, taking small bites and using gentle traction. Widening a small trapdoor by removing a bone fragment is safer than pulling hard on trapped tissue. Watch the heart rate, because traction can set off the oculocardiac reflex and slow the heart.
Size and shape the implant

Measure the defect and trim the implant, such as thin porous polyethylene, a nylon sheet, titanium mesh or a preformed plate. Shape it like a guitar pick to cover the whole defect, resting on stable bone at the front, inner side and back. Contour it to the rise of the floor at the back. Keep it short of the optic canal, about 40 mm behind the rim.
Place the implant

Slide the implant along the floor on a malleable retractor until its back edge rests on the posterior ledge. Make sure no orbital fat or periorbita is trapped under or beside it, and check that the infraorbital nerve is not pinched. Fix it with a screw at the rim if it moves. Many thin sheets stay in place without fixation.
Repeat forced ductions

Repeat forced ductions and compare with the start. Restriction means trapped tissue or a poorly placed implant, so take it out and place it again. Check globe projection and height from above against the other eye. Use image guidance, intraoperative CT or endoscopy to confirm placement in large or posterior defects.
Close

Close the periosteum over the rim with interrupted absorbable sutures so the implant does not move. If a canthotomy was done, reattach the lateral canthal tendon to the inner side of the lateral rim. The conjunctiva can be left to heal or closed loosely with fast-absorbing gut. Some surgeons secure the lid traction suture above the brow for a few days to limit lid retraction.
Postoperative check of vision

Check the pupils for a relative afferent defect before the patient leaves the room, and check vision as soon as the patient is awake. New pain, swelling, a bulging eye or vision loss suggests a hematoma behind the globe and calls for immediate lateral canthotomy with cantholysis and a return to the OR.

steps: Airway and setup

Use nasotracheal intubation so the teeth can be brought together, or submental intubation when nasal intubation is not safe, as with midface or skull-base fractures. Tape the tube away from the field and place a throat pack. Clean the mouth with antiseptic rinse, check every tooth, and keep the CT open to see the roots and the inferior alveolar canal.
Establish the occlusion

Place Erich arch bars with 24- or 26-gauge wires, or MMF screws between the tooth roots. Line up the wear facets of the upper and lower teeth to restore the patient's own bite, not an ideal Class I bite. Use wire loops or elastics for MMF with the condyles seated. In comminuted fractures, reduce the fracture before fully tightening the wires.
Choose the approach

Most symphysis, parasymphysis, body and angle fractures can be reached through the mouth. Use an external approach for a severely comminuted fracture, an edentulous atrophic jaw, or a ramus or condyle fracture. The external options are submandibular, retromandibular or preauricular. Angle fractures can be plated through the mouth with a trocar passed through the cheek.
Intraoral exposure

For anterior fractures, cut through the vestibular mucosa 5 to 10 mm below the gum line, leaving a cuff for closure, and split the mentalis muscle. For the angle, cut along the external oblique ridge, starting low on the front of the ramus. Lift a subperiosteal flap to the lower border of the jaw, and find the mental nerve below the premolars before it is in danger.
External exposure

Make the submandibular cut about two finger widths below the lower border. Go through the platysma, then lift a flap deep to the platysma, below the marginal mandibular nerve and over the facial vessels, using a nerve stimulator when needed. Cut through the pterygomasseteric sling to reach the angle and ramus. The retromandibular approach may go through the parotid.
Clean and reduce

Clear clot and scar from the fracture ends, and remove only bone fragments without soft-tissue attachments. With the teeth in occlusion, reduce the fracture exactly at the lower border using reduction forceps. Make sure the lingual cortex also lines up, because a gap there causes the jaw to splay outward. A tooth in the fracture line that is loose, fractured or infected should come out.
Load-sharing fixation by site

At the angle, place a 2.0 mm miniplate along the external oblique ridge with single-cortex screws (Champy), or use two plates. At the body, place a superior tension-band plate below the tooth roots and an inferior-border plate with screws through both cortices. At the symphysis, use two plates or two lag screws, since twisting forces are highest there.
Protect roots and the nerve

Map the inferior alveolar canal and tooth roots on CT before drilling. Above the canal, use only single-cortex screws, which stay out of the roots. Use screws through both cortices only along the lower border, below the canal. Use a drill guide with irrigation, and choose the screw length from the bone thickness you measure.
Load-bearing fixation when needed

For comminution, bone loss, an atrophic edentulous jaw or an infected fracture, bridge the area with a 2.4 mm locking reconstruction plate. Place at least three, and ideally four, screws through both cortices in solid bone on each side. Bend the plate carefully even with locking screws. Keep the small comminuted pieces attached to soft tissue instead of throwing them away.
Check the occlusion

Release the MMF and move the jaw through opening and closing. The bite should come back the same each time with the condyles seated in their sockets. An open bite, a shift of the midline or early contact means malreduction or a condyle out of place. Remove the plate, reduce the fracture again and refix it rather than accept the bad bite.
Irrigate and close

Irrigate and check for loose hardware, a screw in the canal, or a trapped mental nerve. Close mentalis in its own layer to prevent chin droop, then close the mucosa without tension and watertight with absorbable sutures. For external approaches, close the pterygomasseteric sling, platysma and skin in layers, with a drain if needed.
Postoperative plan

Decide whether to leave arch bars, use guiding elastics or keep MMF. If the jaw is wired, place wire cutters at the bedside and give antiemetics. Record nerve sensation, the diet (soft, no chewing for about 6 weeks), chlorhexidine rinses, and imaging after surgery to confirm the reduction and screw placement.
