steps: Final check before incision

Confirm with ophthalmology the vision, color vision, pupils, eye movements and proptosis just before the case. Review contrast CT for the location and size of the abscess, the sinus source and any spread inside the skull. Load image guidance if available. Place the endoscopy tower at the head of the bed, and leave the eyes taped but visible so the globe can be watched.
Decongest the inflamed mucosa

Inflamed mucosa bleeds a lot. Pack the nose with pledgets soaked in oxymetazoline or epinephrine, and inject lidocaine with epinephrine at the maxillary line, the uncinate and the middle turbinate. Ask for controlled low blood pressure and a slight head-up tilt. Plan the case from easy to hard so the view is clear before you reach the lamina papyracea.
Uncinectomy and maxillary antrostomy

Push the middle turbinate inward, remove the uncinate process, and widen the natural maxillary opening backward and downward. This gives the lowest landmark, the orbital floor at the roof of the maxillary sinus, and removes an infected sinus. Keep this opening clear later if bone over the lower part of the orbit is removed.
Ethmoidectomy along the lamina

Open the ethmoid bulla and the front ethmoid cells, then the back cells if needed. Clear cells along the lamina papyracea from front to back, keeping the skull base above in view. Find the front ethmoid artery. Open the frontal recess or sphenoid only if CT shows they are the source. Take cultures from the sinus pus.
Find the lamina over the abscess

Use image guidance and the CT to line up the abscess, usually along the inner wall of the orbit beside the ethmoid. Gentle pressure on the globe while watching the lamina can show bone that is thin, broken or moving. Pus or granulation coming through the bone confirms where the abscess is.
Remove bone over the abscess

Crack the lamina papyracea with a Cottle or ball-tip probe and lift the bone fragments off the periorbita. Remove a window that covers the full height and length of the collection. Stay below the skull base and the ethmoid arteries. Leave a strip of lamina near the skull base. Do not damage the periorbita while you work.
Drain the subperiosteal collection

A subperiosteal abscess lies between the bone and the periorbita, so removing bone usually releases the pus. Take cultures before irrigating. Spread the pocket gently with a blunt elevator from front to back to break up loculations. Cut the periorbita only for a true orbital abscess within the orbit. Never use a powered tool inside the periorbita.
Protect the medial rectus and orbital apex

Do not suction or grab exposed orbital fat. The medial rectus lies just deep to the medial periorbita. Use only gentle, blunt instruments. Stop dissection well short of the orbital apex and the optic canal behind the posterior ethmoid. Use the posterior ethmoid artery and the sphenoid face as the back limit.
External or combined drainage

If the collection lies above, to the side, far forward, or outside the reach of the endoscope, add an external route. Options are a transcaruncular incision, an upper-lid crease incision, or a Lynch incision. Plan for a soft drain. Involve neurosurgery for any intracranial collection, which may be drained in the same anesthetic.
Irrigate and confirm

Irrigate the sinus cavity and the drained space with saline. Check that the abscess is fully emptied, that the source sinuses drain freely, and that bleeding is controlled. Feel the orbit through the closed lid: it should be softer. Check the pupil before waking the patient.
No tight packing

Avoid tight nasal packing that pushes back on the orbit. Use only light dissolvable material or none. Do not place a pack across the window in the lamina. Make sure anesthesia avoids coughing and straining on emergence, which can cause bleeding into the orbit.
Postoperative eye checks

Recheck vision, pupils and eye movements as soon as the patient is awake and regularly after. Worsening vision, a new afferent pupil defect, a more bulging eye or more limited movement means an orbital emergency. Repeat CT and return to the OR without delay. Continue antibiotics based on cultures with ophthalmology follow-up.

steps: Confirm the plan with endoscopy

Start with laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy under anesthesia. Confirm the Myer-Cotton grade, the length and level of the stenosis, any posterior glottic scar, vocal-fold movement and tracheomalacia. Then confirm whether you need an anterior graft, a posterior graft or both, and whether the reconstruction is single-stage or double-stage. Swap the tracheostomy tube for a sterile tube through the stoma or an endotracheal tube.
Harvest rib cartilage

Through a 3 cm incision just below the right breast (in the fold in girls), expose the longest straight segment of the 4th to 6th costal cartilage. Cut the perichondrium along the upper and lower edges and keep the outer perichondrium on the graft. Dissect behind the cartilage in the plane under the perichondrium, leaving the deep perichondrium to protect the pleura. Remove a 2 to 4 cm segment.
Check the pleura

Fill the donor wound with saline and have anesthesia give a sustained breath. Bubbles mean a pleural tear. Repair it over a red rubber catheter under positive pressure, or place a chest tube. Close the muscle and skin in layers, and plan a chest x-ray. Keep the graft in saline.
Expose the larynx

Make a horizontal neck incision that includes the stoma. Lift subplatysmal flaps, and split the strap muscles in the midline to expose the thyroid cartilage, cricoid and upper tracheal rings. Stay on the front of the framework to protect the recurrent laryngeal nerves, which enter the larynx behind and to the side of the cricoid. Ligate or divide the thyroid isthmus if needed.
Open the airway in the midline

Make a vertical cut strictly in the midline through the upper trachea, the anterior cricoid and the lower third of the thyroid cartilage. Stop below the anterior commissure to protect the voice. Join the cut to the stoma. The cricoid often springs open. Place stay sutures on each cut edge so you can open the airway quickly in an emergency.
Inspect the stenosis

Look directly at the narrowed segment, the posterior glottis and the cricoarytenoid joints. Decide whether the anterior split alone gives enough room or whether the scar or cricoid shape needs a posterior split too. Do not cut out the scar. Expansion with grafts is the aim.
Split the posterior cricoid

For posterior narrowing, inject the posterior cricoid. Divide the scar and the full height of the cricoid plate exactly in the midline down to the mucosa of the hypopharynx, but not through it. Extend the cut upward into the interarytenoid muscle only if it is scarred, and downward about 1 cm into the wall between the trachea and esophagus. Spread the halves apart.
Carve the grafts

Shape an anterior graft into a boat shape with edges that sit on the outside of the cut cartilage so it cannot fall into the airway. Shape a posterior graft as a T or rectangle with flanges that slip into pockets under the mucosa behind the cricoid halves. Keep the perichondrium facing the inside of the airway. Size the graft to widen the airway without tension.
Place the posterior graft

Wedge the posterior graft between the split halves of the cricoid plate with the flanges locked behind the cut edges. Suture it with fine absorbable sutures if it is not stable. Make sure it sits level with the inner surface and does not stick out into the esophagus or the airway.
Stent or tube

For a single-stage repair, pass a nasotracheal tube of the size planned past the repair to act as the stent. For a double-stage repair, place a stent (such as a suprastomal stent or Aboulker stent) above the tracheostomy tube and secure it. The tube or stent must not press too hard on the grafts.
Place the anterior graft

Parachute the boat-shaped graft into the anterior opening with the perichondrium facing the inside. Sew it with interrupted absorbable sutures that do not pass into the airway. The flanges should rest on the outside of the cartilage. Check from above with a telescope that the graft sits level and does not drop into the airway.
Leak test, close and drain

Fill the wound with saline and have anesthesia give positive pressure with the tube cuff let down. Fix any air leak. Close the strap muscles over the graft and close the skin loosely around a drain so trapped air can escape. Confirm the tube or stent position with a scope and chest x-ray, then transfer to the ICU.

steps: Mark and infiltrate

With the patient asleep, re-mark dorsal lines, tip-defining points and planned osteotomy paths. Place oxymetazoline pledgets, then infiltrate lidocaine with epinephrine in the subperichondrial septal plane, along the dorsum and tip, and along the lateral osteotomy tracks. Wait for full vasoconstriction before incising, which makes plane identification and flap elevation easier.
Choose and open the approach

Use an open approach (stair-step transcolumellar incision joined to bilateral marginal incisions along the caudal edge of the lower lateral cartilages) when middle-vault or tip grafts must be sutured. Use a hemitransfixion or Killian incision alone for septum-only work. Raise the skin envelope just above the perichondrium and beneath the periosteum over the bones.
Elevate septal flaps

Reach the caudal septum through the hemitransfixion incision or from above by separating the upper lateral cartilages from the dorsal septum. Raise mucoperichondrium with a Cottle elevator in the bloodless subperichondrial plane, then elevate the floor subperiosteally from the piriform aperture. Join floor and septal tunnels over crest spurs, where thin mucosa tears most easily.
Define the L-strut

Mark dorsal and caudal limbs of at least 1 cm (many surgeons keep about 1.5 cm), keeping the caudal limb attached at the nasal spine and the dorsal limb intact at the keystone. Remove only the cartilage that obstructs or is needed for grafts; routinely taking all cartilage outside the strut is unnecessary and weakens support.
Resect and harvest cartilage

Incise the quadrangular cartilage with the Cottle at the bony-cartilaginous junction, staying behind the planned L-strut. Remove it in one piece with wide-mouthed forceps so it stays usable for grafts. Before taking deviated perpendicular plate or vomer, make a controlled superior cut with Becker scissors; never twist bone high on the septum, which risks a cribriform plate fracture and CSF leak.
Correct crest and caudal deviation

Free the septum from the maxillary crest trough. Shave a one-sided crest spur with a small osteotome or excise a deviated crest segment while keeping the nasal spine. For a caudal septum off the crest, use a swinging-door maneuver: free it, reset it in the midline groove and suture it to spine periosteum with long-lasting absorbable suture.
Straighten the remaining strut

Address residual bowing of the L-strut with conservative scoring of the concave side, splinting grafts of thin septal cartilage or perforated perpendicular plate, or a dorsal crossbar graft on the concave side. Stabilize every segment so fragments cannot overlap. Severe twisting of the whole caudal septum may need caudal replacement or extracorporeal septoplasty.
Manage the dorsum

Separate the upper lateral cartilages from the septum without tearing underlying mucosa, then reduce the cartilaginous septum incrementally with a scalpel and the bony hump with a rasp or osteotome. Check the profile repeatedly. Over-reduction of the cartilaginous dorsum both creates a saddle and narrows the internal valve, so preserve or rebuild the junction.
Rebuild the internal valve

Restore the middle vault with spreader grafts of septal cartilage placed between the dorsal septum and each upper lateral cartilage and fixed with horizontal mattress sutures of 5-0 PDS, or with autospreader (turn-in) flaps when the upper laterals are long enough. Flaring sutures can widen the valve angle further. Confirm the dorsal aesthetic lines remain smooth and symmetric.
Support the tip and external valve

Set tip support with a columellar strut or caudal septal extension graft sutured between the medial crura. Correct lateral wall or external valve collapse with lateral crural strut grafts, alar batten grafts shaped convex outward and placed in a precise pocket at the point of maximal collapse, or alar rim grafts. Avoid over-rotation and nostril distortion.
Perform osteotomies last

Use 2- to 3-mm micro-osteotomes after all other work is finished. Start the lateral osteotomy at the piriform aperture at or just above the inferior turbinate, preserving the bony triangle along the nasal floor, then curve along the nasomaxillary groove to meet a medial oblique cut. Infracture gently with finger pressure and hold pressure over the sites.
Reassess structure and airway

Palpate the dorsum for steps and irregularities, recheck that the septum sits midline on the crest and that the strut is firm, and confirm valve patency by inspection and with the endoscope. Treat contributing inferior turbinate hypertrophy now if planned, using outfracture or submucous reduction that spares mucosa.
Close the septum

Return crushed, straightened leftover cartilage between the flaps to support them. Repair every mucosal tear, even one-sided, with 5-0 plain gut so tears do not become a perforation. Place a continuous quilting suture through both flaps on a curved needle to close dead space and prevent hematoma, then close the hemitransfixion incision without cutting the alar facet.
Close skin and splint

Close the columellar incision with fine permanent monofilament and the marginal incisions with absorbable suture, redraping the skin evenly. Place silicone intranasal splints when the septum was extensively reworked or mucosa was torn, then tape the dorsum and tip and apply an external splint. Document airway findings and the grafts used.

steps: Measure and mark

Measure helix-to-mastoid distances at the superior, middle and inferior thirds on both sides (roughly 10 to 12, 16 to 18 and 20 to 22 mm in a normal ear). Fold the ear by hand to simulate the antihelix, then mark planned mattress-suture points through the skin and cartilage with a needle dipped in methylene blue.
Infiltrate and excise skin

Infiltrate the postauricular skin with local anesthetic containing epinephrine. Excise a fusiform ellipse of postauricular skin sized by holding the ear in its intended position, placed eccentrically on the back of the pinna so the scar settles into the sulcus. Remove skin conservatively, because skin excision alone does not hold correction.
Expose the posterior cartilage

Elevate the posterior skin over the perichondrium laterally toward the helical rim and medially to the mastoid. Keep the perichondrium on the cartilage for suture purchase. Stay superficial near the lobule to protect the great auricular nerve branches, and keep hemostasis precise with bipolar cautery.
Clear the postauricular bed

Excise the posterior auricular muscle and the soft tissue between the conchal bowl and the mastoid to create space for the concha to sit back. Expose a broad area of mastoid periosteum as the anchor for conchal sutures. This soft-tissue removal often produces a substantial part of the setback.
Set back the concha

Place Furnas-type horizontal mattress sutures of clear permanent material from the conchal cartilage (cymba, cavum and fossa triangularis region as needed) to mastoid periosteum. Pull posteriorly and slightly superiorly so the concha does not narrow the external canal, and do not overcorrect the middle third, which produces a telephone-ear deformity.
Reduce a deep bowl

When the conchal wall is very tall or the bowl very deep despite sutures, excise a crescent of cartilage from the posterior conchal wall or shave the conchal eminence. Keep the anterior skin intact and avoid sharp cartilage edges that would be visible or palpable through the thin anterior skin.
Weaken stiff cartilage

For thick, springy cartilage that will not fold with sutures alone, soften the anterior surface along the planned antihelix by abrasion or light scoring through a small access point, or score from behind with a needle. Score only as much as needed; deep or uneven scoring produces sharp ridges and irregular contour.
Create the antihelical fold

Place three or four Mustardé-type horizontal mattress sutures across the planned fold, taking bites of about 4 to 6 mm through cartilage and anterior perichondrium without entering the anterior skin. Hold each with a clamp, then tie in order after simulating the fold, setting tension for a smoothly rolled antihelix rather than a sharp crease.
Correct the superior pole

If the upper pole remains prominent after the antihelix is formed, add a suture from the scapha or fossa triangularis to the temporalis fascia or deep tissue above the mastoid. Without this the upper third may stay prominent while the middle third sits back, mimicking a telephone ear.
Correct the lobule

Address a prominent lobule last, because conchal setback often changes its position. Options include excising a fishtail of skin on the back of the lobule with a dermal-to-concha or mastoid suture, or repositioning the cauda helicis. Aim for a lobule that follows the line of the corrected helix.
Check symmetry

Compare both ears from frontal, lateral and posterior views. The helical rim should remain visible just behind the antihelix from the front, with a smooth, continuous profile from superior pole to lobule. Remeasure the three distances; side differences of about 2 to 3 mm are acceptable. Adjust or replace sutures before closure.
Close the incision

Confirm hemostasis, then close the skin with interrupted absorbable sutures, leaving tiny gaps so blood can drain. Ensure no permanent knot sits under thin skin or along the suture line, where it may extrude. Avoid closing under tension, which widens the scar and pulls the ear.
Apply the dressing

Mold cotton soaked in mineral oil into the conchal bowl, scapha and helical folds to support contour, then apply fluffs and a mastoid-type head dressing that is snug but not compressive. Plan an early check, usually the next day, to inspect for hematoma before the patient leaves the dressing in place.

setup: Before otoplasty, analyze the specific deformity—underdeveloped antihelical fold, conchal excess/depth, lobular prominence, asymmetry or a combination—and match the correction to that anatomy rather than applying one maneuver to every prominent ear. Document baseline asymmetry and skin/cartilage quality and plan correction that avoids over-set ears or excessive conchal-mastoid narrowing.
Measure and photograph helix-to-mastoid distances at the upper, middle and lower thirds and the conchomastoid angle on both sides for planning and documentation.

Plan the sequence of maneuvers (conchal setback and antihelical fold in a consistent order, with the lobule addressed last) and have permanent clear sutures (for example 4-0 nylon or polyester), a cartilage scorer or rasp, and a bolster or head dressing ready.

steps: Make the subunit template

Analyze the defect by subunit. When much of a convex subunit such as the tip or ala is missing, enlarge the defect to the subunit borders and discard the remnant. Make a foil or suture-pack template of the ideal subunit, using the contralateral side as the guide, so the flap restores the intended contour rather than just filling the hole.
Restore lining first

Rebuild missing internal lining before cover. Options include turnover hinge flaps of adjacent skin, a bipedicle vestibular skin advancement flap for small caudal defects, an ipsilateral septal mucoperichondrial hinge flap, a folded distal forehead flap or a skin graft for small areas. Lining that is thin and vascular supports cartilage grafts and prevents contraction.
Place cartilage support

Add primary framework grafts before cover: septal or conchal cartilage battens along the alar margin even where the ala normally lacks cartilage, tip and dome grafts, and septal, rib or calvarial grafts for dorsal support. Suture them firmly in place so the overlying skin does not collapse or retract the rim during healing.
Design the pedicle

Confirm the supratrochlear vessels with Doppler, usually 1.7 to 2.2 cm from the midline at the medial brow, typically on the side of most of the defect. Center a 1.2 to 1.5 cm pedicle on the vessel. Measure length with a suture from the pivot point to the farthest defect point, then place the template, angling it along the hairline if needed to avoid hair.
Elevate the distal flap

Incise around the template and raise the distal 1 to 2 cm in a subcutaneous plane, or with a thin layer of frontalis in smokers. Proceed into the subgaleal plane over the mid-forehead, which is relatively bloodless and keeps the axial vessels in the flap. Keep incisions perpendicular so edges match the nasal skin.
Free the pedicle at the brow

Near the brow, change to blunt and subperiosteal dissection within about 2 cm of the orbital rim to protect the supratrochlear vessels. Divide the corrugator fibers that tether the pedicle to gain movement, and extend the pedicle incisions below the brow if extra length is needed. Avoid narrowing, skeletonizing or cauterizing near the vessels.
Thin the flap

Sculpt the distal portion to the thickness of the recipient nasal skin by removing frontalis and subcutaneous fat; in suitable nonsmokers nearly all fat beneath the dermis can be removed distally. Leave the proximal portion thick for later thinning. Thin more conservatively in smokers, diabetics and irradiated patients to protect the subdermal plexus.
Transpose the flap

Rotate the flap medially and down to the nose, checking that the pedicle is not twisted, kinked or under tension. Confirm brisk bleeding from the distal edge. If the flap is short or blanches under tension, gain length by dissecting further below the brow rather than accepting tension at the inset.
Inset the flap

Suture the flap precisely to the subunit borders with fine deep sutures and everted skin closure, matching the template outline. Join the lining to the flap margin where full-thickness repair was needed. Avoid tension along the alar margin, which can cause notching, and keep the edges perpendicular to limit trapdoor contracture.
Close the donor site

Undermine the forehead widely in the subgaleal plane, from the edge of one temporalis to the other. Add parallel vertical galeal scoring 2 to 3 cm apart if needed, then close in layers. Leave any upper portion that will not close to heal by secondary intention, kept moist with ointment; this usually gives an acceptable scar.
Dress the pedicle

Cover the raw undersurface of the pedicle with ointment-impregnated gauze or a thin skin graft to limit bleeding and crusting. Confirm flap color and capillary refill, and apply a light dressing with nothing pressing on the pedicle. Teach the patient daily care and warning signs of congestion or bleeding.
Intermediate stage when needed

For complex full-thickness repairs, consider a three-stage plan: at about 3 weeks, re-elevate the flap off the nose except at the pedicle, sculpt soft tissue and adjust cartilage grafts, then return it. Divide the pedicle about 3 weeks later. This improves contour where a single thinning would endanger the flap.
Divide the pedicle

At about 3 weeks (later in smokers or after radiation), under local anesthesia, divide the pedicle, thin the remaining proximal flap and undermine the nasal skin above the inset about 1 cm to insert the superior edge. Return only a small inverted triangle to the brow to restore its position; discard excess rather than placing it above the brow.
Refine later

Wait at least several months for scar maturation before refinements. Address residual bulk, trapdoor contour or edge irregularities with debulking through existing scars, dermabrasion or scar revision. Treat any hair-bearing skin transferred to the nose with depilation. Assess the airway and alar position at each visit.
forehead-flap.source_label: Cummings 7e (Reconstruction of Facial Defects) and Pasha 6e

steps: Confirm the plan at the table

Before incision, match the technique to the collapse pattern: expansion sphincter or lateral pharyngoplasty for lateral wall narrowing, a conservative uvulopalatopharyngoplasty variant or uvulopalatal flap for anteroposterior collapse, and Z-palatoplasty for a scarred or webbed palate after prior surgery. Confirm any planned nasal or tongue-base procedures and their order.
Position and expose

With an oral tube secured in the midline, place a shoulder roll and suspend a mouth gag carefully, avoiding excessive opening and tongue compression. Inspect the palate length and thickness, pillar web and tonsil size, and palpate the pterygoid hamulus on each side as the landmark for palatal fixation. Infiltrate pillars and palate with dilute epinephrine.
Remove the tonsils

Perform extracapsular tonsillectomy, keeping the dissection on the capsule and preserving as much anterior and posterior pillar mucosa and muscle as possible, especially the palatopharyngeus. Control bleeding with bipolar or suction cautery as you go, avoiding deep coagulation of the constrictor that adds pain and scar.
Identify the palatopharyngeus

Within the posterior pillar, define the vertical fibers of the palatopharyngeus and separate them from the underlying superior constrictor. Keep the dissection on the muscle surface so the constrictor and the glossopharyngeal nerve near the lower pole are not injured.
Divide the muscle low

Transect the palatopharyngeus horizontally at its inferior portion, roughly two thirds of the way down its length, keeping the superior end attached to the palate. Dissect the mobilized muscle off the constrictor from below upward. Leaving its upper attachment intact keeps the muscle vascularized and innervated from above.
Make the palatal tunnel

Make a small incision in the anterior soft palate superolateral to the tonsil fossa, in line with the hamulus and the arch of the pterygomandibular raphe. Create a submucosal tunnel from this incision down to the upper tonsil fossa, wide enough to pass the muscle without strangling it.
Rotate and suspend

Pass the free end of the palatopharyngeus superolaterally through the tunnel and secure it with an absorbable figure-of-eight suture to the fibrous tissue of the palatal arch near the hamulus and raphe. The pull should visibly widen the lateral retropalatal airway; tie with enough tension to hold the muscle without cutting through it.
Repeat on the other side

Perform the same mobilization and suspension contralaterally, matching tension and position so the palate is not pulled to one side. Compare the width of the lateral ports and the position of the uvula. Asymmetry now tends to persist as asymmetric scar.
Close the pillars

Approximate the anterior pillar to the remaining posterior pillar tissue with absorbable sutures, obliterating the tonsil fossa dead space without tight tension. Close the small palatal incisions. Avoid excessive closure that tethers the palate downward, which can reduce velar mobility and contribute to velopharyngeal insufficiency.
Trim the uvula conservatively

If the uvula is long and redundant, trim only its tip and leave enough length and muscle to preserve velopharyngeal closure. Do not resect palate muscle aggressively. Overresection of the soft palate is the main source of hypernasal speech, nasal regurgitation and nasopharyngeal stenosis after palatal surgery.
Inspect with the gag relaxed

Release suspension and look again at the retropalatal airway, palate symmetry, uvular position and suture lines. Retract the palate to view the nasopharynx and confirm the closure did not create a web. Replace sutures that cut through or leave raw areas.
Secure hemostasis and finish

Check both fossae and suture lines under a raised airway pressure maneuver, then suction the nasopharynx and stomach. Remove the gag, check the teeth and lips, and extubate fully awake. Arrange monitored observation and a steroid and analgesic plan matched to sleep apnea severity, opioid exposure and comorbidity.
reconstructive-palate.source_label: Cummings 7e (Sleep Apnea and Sleep Disorders) and K.J. Lee (Obstructive Sleep Apnea)

steps: Plan the osteotomy

On the panoramic radiograph or CT, measure canine and incisor root length and mandibular height, and locate the genial tubercle on the lingual cortex. Plan a rectangular window that captures the tubercle, with the superior cut several millimeters below the root apices and an intact inferior border of about 1 cm. Secure the airway with an anesthetic plan suited to sleep apnea.
Open the vestibule

Make a labial vestibular incision well away from the gingiva, leaving a cuff of mucosa and mentalis for a layered closure. Divide the mentalis and elevate subperiosteally over the anterior mandible. Identify both mental foramina below the premolars and keep the dissection and the osteotomy well medial to them.
Confirm the tubercle

Palpate the genial tubercle through the floor of the mouth or along the lingual cortex and correlate with the imaging to confirm the window is centered on it. Mark the four cuts on the outer cortex with a bur. If the tubercle sits high, narrow the window rather than cutting closer to the root apices.
Place a handle screw

Before completing the cuts, place a screw in the center of the planned segment to serve as a handle for controlling and advancing the fragment. This keeps the segment from dropping into the floor of the mouth and allows gentle traction without disrupting the muscle attachments.
Cut the window

Make the rectangular osteotomy through both cortices with a fine saw or bur under irrigation. Keep the lateral cuts medial to the canine roots, the superior cut below the apices and the inferior cut above the preserved border. Finish the lingual cortex carefully so the saw does not plunge into the floor of the mouth and injure vessels.
Advance the genial segment

Pull the segment forward with the handle screw, releasing only periosteal attachments while keeping the genioglossus and geniohyoid on the bone. The advancement is roughly the thickness of the mandible. Check the floor of the mouth for bleeding, which can expand into a dangerous hematoma if missed.
Rotate and fix

Rotate the segment so its lingual cortex rests on the outer cortex of the mandible below the window, then secure it with one or two screws into the inferior symphysis. Remove the outer cortex and marrow of the projecting segment with a bur to limit a chin bulge, and confirm the fixation is rigid.
Close the mouth

Irrigate, resuspend the mentalis to prevent lower-lip ptosis, and close the mucosa in layers with absorbable sutures. Apply a supportive chin dressing. Recheck tongue position and the floor of the mouth before moving to the neck.
Expose the hyoid

Make a horizontal incision in a skin crease over the hyoid, raise subplatysmal flaps and expose the hyoid body and the medial part of each greater cornu. Stay on bone and medial; the hypoglossal nerve and lingual artery run above the greater cornu and the superior laryngeal neurovascular bundle lies near its tip and the thyrohyoid membrane.
Release the infrahyoid muscles

For hyothyroidopexy, divide the infrahyoid strap muscles from the inferior border of the hyoid body to free it, leaving the suprahyoid musculature intact. Mobilize only as much as the planned movement requires. Over-releasing the hyoid and its suprahyoid attachments adds dysphagia without improving the airway.
Suspend the hyoid

Expose the upper thyroid cartilage, then pass two to four permanent sutures or wires around the hyoid body and through the thyroid laminae on each side of the midline. Tie them symmetrically to bring the hyoid forward and down over the thyroid notch. In hyomandibular suspension the vector is instead forward and upward to the mandible.
Check and close

Confirm the hyoid sits symmetrically without excessive downward displacement of the larynx, check neck and floor-of-mouth hemostasis, and place a drain when the dead space is large. Close the platysma and skin in layers. Review all sites for bleeding and fixation integrity before emergence.
Plan the recovery

Extubate fully awake and observe in a monitored setting matched to apnea severity, opioid needs and the extent of multilevel surgery. Start a soft diet with oral rinses, test lower-lip sensation and swallowing early, and schedule follow-up for tooth vitality, wound healing and repeat objective sleep testing after recovery.
hyoid-genioglossus.source_label: Cummings 7e (Sleep Apnea and Sleep Disorders) and K.J. Lee (Obstructive Sleep Apnea)

steps: Classify on CT

Using thin-cut CT in all planes, define the central fragment and whether the medial canthal tendon sits on a large piece (type I), a comminuted but usable piece (type II), or is detached or on unusable fragments (type III). Note medial wall, floor, frontal sinus outflow and skull-base injury, and plan repair early, before swelling and scarring make reduction difficult.
Expose the region

Use a coronal incision for bilateral or comminuted injuries, raised subgaleally and then subperiosteally a few centimeters above the rims, staying deep to the superficial layer of deep temporal fascia to protect the frontal branch. Add transconjunctival or subciliary and maxillary vestibular incisions, or use existing lacerations, for the inferior rim and piriform aperture.
Free the supraorbital bundle

Release the supraorbital neurovascular bundle from its notch, or from a foramen with a small osteotome, so the periosteum can be lowered over the nasal root. Continue subperiosteal dissection down the nasal bones, frontal process of the maxilla and medial orbit, keeping the dissection off the canthal insertion on the central fragment.
Identify the canthal tendon

Locate the medial canthal tendon and lacrimal sac. From the front, press a clamp into the tissue near the caruncle; the indentation seen from the coronal side shows where the tendon can be found and grasped. Decide whether the tendon remains on a fragment that can be plated or wired, or needs direct canthopexy.
Address frontal sinus and skull base

Establish a stable upper reference first. With neurosurgery, repair dural tears and CSF leak, and manage the frontal sinus according to posterior table and outflow injury. Reconstruct the frontal bar and nasal root so the central fragment and nasal bones have a solid platform to reduce against.
Plate a type I fragment

Reduce the single large central fragment in three dimensions to the frontal bone above, the infraorbital rim and piriform aperture below. Fix it with microplates, keeping hardware off the canthal insertion. Incomplete or loose fixation lets the fragment slowly drift laterally, which produces late telecanthus.
Wire a type II fragment

When the tendon-bearing fragment is too small for plates, drill holes in it and pass a fine wire transnasally to the opposite side, placing the wire posterior and superior to the lacrimal fossa. Tightening this wire draws the fragment back and medially. Alternatively, free the tendon and treat the injury as type III.
Canthopexy for type III

Tag the tendon with permanent suture or wire and pass it with an awl from the region of the posterior lacrimal crest, behind the nasal bones and through the septum, to the other side. Shield the contralateral globe with a broad retractor. Anchor it to a contralateral frontal screw, plate or tendon, pulling posteriorly, superiorly and medially.
Rebuild the medial orbital wall

Reconstruct a deficient medial wall or floor with bone graft or an implant before tightening transnasal fixation, so the canthus has a posterior structure to sit against. A drill hole in the graft allows correct passage of the transnasal wire. Check forced ductions after placement.
Restore dorsal height

If nasal dorsal height or support is lost, place a cantilevered calvarial bone graft fixed at the radix with a plate or lag screw. Restoring projection prevents a saddle deformity and reduces the risk of epicanthal folds that accompany a flattened nasal root.
Manage the lacrimal system

Probe the canaliculi when injury is suspected and repair lacerations over silicone stents. A bony nasolacrimal duct injury is usually observed at first, accepting that persistent epiphora may need later dacryocystorhinostomy. Avoid placing wires or screws through the lacrimal fossa.
Tighten and check

Tighten the transnasal fixation after the bony framework is set. Measure intercanthal distance, aiming for about half the interpupillary distance with slight overcorrection, and compare canthal height and depth on both sides. Repeat the bowstring test, check globe position and confirm no CSF leak.
Redrape the soft tissue

Resuspend the periosteum and midface soft tissues to their attachments and secure the temporal fascia. Medial canthal soft-tissue bolsters or external nasal splints may help restore the natural concavity, although their value is uncertain. Close the coronal flap over a drain and the other incisions in layers.
noe-orif.source_label: Cummings 7e (Maxillofacial Trauma) and K.J. Lee (Craniomaxillofacial Trauma)

attending_followup: How is medial canthal tendon stability assessed, and why does it matter?

With the bowstring test (lateral traction on the lower lid while palpating the canthus) plus CT; swelling alone is unreliable. Missing an unstable tendon leads to permanent telecanthus that needs formal transnasal canthopexy.
What does the Markowitz-Manson classification describe?

Type I is a single large central fragment with the tendon attached, which is plated; type II is a comminuted central fragment with the tendon still on a usable piece, which usually needs transnasal wiring of that fragment; and type III is comminution into the tendon insertion or tendon detachment, which needs transnasal canthopexy of the tendon itself.
What is the target intercanthal distance?
About half the interpupillary distance (roughly 30 to 35 mm in adults); over 35 mm suggests and over 40 mm confirms telecanthus.

steps: Confirm the defect fits

After clear margins, measure the defect and confirm it is about 1.5 cm or smaller, at least about 5 mm from the alar rim, and has intact perichondrium. Pinch the upper sidewall and dorsum to confirm a skin reservoir. Larger, deeper or rim-involving defects are better served by a melolabial or forehead flap or a composite repair.
Choose the base

Orient the flap to recruit loose skin from the upper sidewall and dorsum. Medial tip defects generally take a laterally based flap, and lateral tip or alar defects a medially based flap. Plan the second-lobe donor where its closure will not pull the alar rim upward or distort the medial canthus.
Mark the pivot and arcs

Place the pivot point one defect radius from the defect edge. From it, draw one arc through the center of the defect and a second at the far edge of the defect. These arcs set the height of each lobe so both reach far enough without excess, keeping rotation and the standing cones small.
Draw the lobes

Draw the first lobe the same width as the defect on the thick tip skin, and the second lobe narrower, about half to three quarters of the first, ending in a point so its donor closes in a line. Keep each lobe's rotation to about 45 to 50 degrees, about 90 to 100 degrees in total.
Mark the Burow triangle

Mark a triangle of skin between the defect and the pivot point for excision. Removing it at the start takes away the standing cone that would otherwise form at the pivot, where it is the most visible and hardest to correct later.
Infiltrate and incise

Infiltrate local anesthetic with epinephrine around the defect and design, and wait for vasoconstriction. Excise the Burow triangle and incise both lobes vertically through skin and subcutaneous tissue down to the nasalis, keeping the edges perpendicular to limit trapdoor contracture.
Elevate beneath the nasalis

Raise the flap in the submuscular plane, beneath the nasalis and directly on perichondrium and periosteum. This plane bleeds little, keeps the flap thick and well perfused, and lets the skin and muscle move as one unit. Avoid thinning the flap, which increases distal necrosis risk.
Undermine widely

Undermine in the same plane around the defect, the pivot, both donor sites and across the dorsum and lateral sidewall to the nasofacial junction. Broad undermining spreads tension across the nose and is the main defense against pincushioning. Control bleeding with bipolar cautery, sparing the flap base.
Close the second donor first

Close the second-lobe donor defect first with a deep absorbable suture. This is the key tension-bearing closure; it brings the lobes into place and reveals whether the alar rim or canthus is being pulled. If the rim lifts, revise the design before going further.
Transpose and trim the lobes

Transpose the first lobe into the primary defect and the second into the first-lobe donor. Trim each to fit the defect exactly; excess tissue left in the defect produces bulging and trapdoor contour. Trim any remaining standing cone conservatively only after the lobes are seated and perfusion is confirmed.
Place deep sutures

Place fine absorbable buried dermal sutures to carry tension and align the lobes, keeping the knots away from the pivot to avoid strangling the base. Make sure tension runs across the nose rather than vertically toward the alar margin, which can cause rim retraction.
Close the skin

Close the epidermis with fine permanent or fast-absorbing sutures with careful edge eversion. Keep the epidermal closure light around the flap base and tip of the second lobe, the most vulnerable areas, and avoid tight sutures that blanch the skin.
Final check and dressing

Inspect the alar rims and nostrils for symmetry and notching, confirm color and capillary refill at the tips of both lobes, and look for residual standing cones at the pivot and second donor. Apply a light, noncompressive dressing and arrange suture removal at about 5 to 7 days.
bilobed-flap.source_label: Pasha 6e and Cummings 7e (Reconstruction of Facial Defects)

setup: Confirm the defect is suitable: lower-third nasal skin defect up to about 1.5 cm, at least about 5 mm from the alar rim, with perichondrium intact or only minor cartilage loss.
Check the skin reservoir over the upper sidewall and dorsum by pinching; thick, sebaceous tip skin and thin dorsal skin affect contour match and pincushioning risk.

Decide the flap base: medial tip defects generally use a laterally based flap and lateral tip or alar defects a medially based flap; plan the second-lobe donor where closure will not pull the ala or medial canthus.
Have a ruler, marking pen, fine skin hooks, and absorbable deep and fine permanent or fast-absorbing skin sutures ready.

steps: Define the defect and subunits

Once margins are clear, decide what cover, lining and support are missing. If more than half of the alar subunit is gone, consider excising the remainder and resurfacing the whole ala. Treat any cheek part separately: close the medial cheek with a cheek advancement flap so its border recreates the alar-facial sulcus, and use the melolabial flap for the nose only.
Choose one or two stages

Use a superiorly based one-stage transposition flap for sidewall and small lateral alar defects, accepting some blunting of the alar-facial sulcus. Use a superiorly based interpolated flap for full alar subunit or rim defects so the sulcus is preserved. Reserve inferiorly based designs for upper lip, nasal sill and columella defects.
Make the template

Cut a foil or suture-packet template of the defect, or of the ideal contralateral subunit when resurfacing the whole ala. Pivot it on gauze from the planned pedicle near the alar base to confirm reach without tension, adding a few millimeters of length for the arc of rotation and the bulk of any cartilage graft.
Mark the flap on the cheek

Place the medial border of the flap exactly in the melolabial crease so the donor scar hides there, with the distal flap in the lower fold where skin is most redundant. Taper the inferior end for a clean closure, and check in men that beard-bearing skin will not be carried onto the nose.
Restore lining and support first

For full-thickness alar defects up to about 1.5 cm high, advance a bipedicle vestibular skin flap for lining; larger defects need septal mucosal hinge flaps. Then place auricular or septal cartilage grafts, including a batten along the nostril margin below the original lateral crus position even when no cartilage was lost, to prevent notching and retraction.
Incise and elevate the distal flap

Infiltrate local anesthetic with epinephrine. Incise through skin and elevate the distal two thirds of the flap in the subcutaneous fat, superficial to the mimetic muscles, at an even depth. Avoid buttonholing, because the distal flap will later be thinned close to the dermis along the rim.
Develop the pedicle

For an interpolated flap, base the proximal flap on a subcutaneous tissue pedicle near the alar base that carries perforators from the facial and angular arteries; it pivots more freely than a skin pedicle and wastes less upper-fold skin. Keep it generously wide and deep enough to rotate without kinking, and never skeletonize it to gain reach.
Thin the flap to fit

Thin the distal flap so it drapes over the cartilage grafts and recreates the alar lobule and crease, down to dermis only along the rim. Leave the proximal third with ample fat to protect perfusion. If the flap pales or bleeds dark after thinning, stop and leave further contouring for the second stage.
Inset the flap

Transfer the interpolated flap over the intact alar-facial sulcus and inset it with a few buried absorbable sutures and fine cutaneous sutures. When the rim and vestibule are involved, sew the inferior flap edge to the vestibular lining flap. Avoid inset tension that lifts the rim, and confirm the pedicle has not twisted.
Close the donor site

Undermine the cheek in the subcutaneous plane and advance it to close along the melolabial crease, excising the inferior standing cone in line with the fold. Use deep sutures to keep tension off the lip and commissure, and anchor the deep tissue to recreate the fold if it has flattened.
Dress the pedicle and check perfusion

Cover the raw undersurface of the pedicle with ointment or petrolatum gauze and avoid any dressing pressure on it. Confirm color and capillary refill at the distal flap before leaving the room, and evacuate any hematoma now rather than leave pressure under a random-pattern tip.
Divide and inset at the second stage

At about 3 weeks, under local anesthesia, divide the pedicle, thin the proximal flap of fat and scar, and inset it to define the alar-facial groove. Discard the pedicle base or return a small part of it to the cheek and close the crease primarily. Plan later revision for trapdoor bulk or notching.
melolabial-flap.source_label: Cummings 7e Ch 21 (Reconstruction of Facial Defects) and Pasha 6e Ch 8

attending_followup: What threatens flap survival and alar contour?
A narrow or twisted pedicle threatens perfusion, while inset tension or missing cartilage support lifts or notches the ala. Keep a broad subcutaneous base and place a rim batten graft.
When choose an interpolated two-stage flap?
For full alar subunit defects, where an interpolated flap preserves the alar-facial groove; divide at about 3 weeks after neovascularization.
Why superiorly based for the nose and inferiorly based for the lip?

The pivot must sit near the defect: a superior base at the alar base reaches the ala and the lower two thirds of the nasal sidewall, while an inferior base reaches the upper lip, nasal sill and columella.

steps: Confirm margins and plan the vector

Reconstruct only after margins are clear, ideally with frozen-section or Mohs control, because the flap rearranges tissue widely. Measure the defect and pick the rotation: an anteriorly based flap recruiting lateral cheek and neck skin for medial and infraorbital defects, or a posteriorly or inferiorly based design for lateral cheek and preauricular defects.
Assess and protect the lower lid

Test lower-lid laxity with snap-back and distraction tests before incising. A lax lid, common in older patients, will be pulled down by the flap, so plan a lateral canthopexy or tarsal strip at the same sitting and plan suspension to the lateral orbital rim periosteum.
Mark the incisions on subunit borders

From the superior edge of the defect, follow the infraorbital rim or lid-cheek junction laterally, rising above the level of the lateral canthus toward the temple. Descend in the preauricular crease, around the lobule and into the neck as far as reach requires, along the anterior border of trapezius toward the clavicle for very large flaps.
Infiltrate and incise

Infiltrate the incision line and dissection plane with dilute local anesthetic with epinephrine to reduce bleeding and help open the plane. Incise through dermis into subcutaneous fat, starting at the defect, and bevel parallel to the follicles in the hair-bearing temple to avoid alopecia along the scar.
Elevate the facial portion

Raise the cheek in the subcutaneous plane superficial to the SMAS, leaving an even layer of fat on the flap. Over the parotid a sub-SMAS (deep-plane) dissection is safe and improves perfusion in smokers or irradiated skin; anterior to the gland, where facial nerve branches become superficial, come up and stay superficial to the SMAS and zygomaticus major.
Protect the parotid, duct and great auricular nerve

Stay on the parotid fascia without entering the gland, which risks sialocele, and avoid the parotid duct along the line from tragus to mid upper lip as dissection crosses the anterior masseter. As you pass the lobule, identify the great auricular nerve on sternocleidomastoid and keep it down with the deep tissue.
Extend into the neck beneath platysma

Below the mandible, move into the subplatysmal plane so the platysma carries blood supply with the flap and shields the marginal mandibular branch, which lies just deep to it near the facial vessels. Continue inferiorly until the flap advances into the defect without tension, extending toward the clavicle if needed.
Gain length without narrowing the base

Undermine widely and test the advance repeatedly. If more reach is needed, extend the incision further inferiorly rather than narrowing the base. A small back-cut is acceptable only if the base stays broad, because this random-pattern flap depends on facial and submental perforators entering through its base.
Suspend the flap to bone

Rotate and advance the flap, then place the main tension on deep permanent or slowly absorbable sutures from the flap undersurface to the periosteum of the infraorbital rim, zygoma or lateral orbital rim. The skin edges should then meet with almost no tension and the lower lid should not be pulled down.
Check the lid and commissure

Inspect the lower lid with the eyes open and closed for scleral show, rounding or eversion. Perform a lateral canthopexy or tarsal strip if the lid is lax or pulled down, and confirm the oral commissure and melolabial fold sit symmetrically before closing.
Excise standing cones last

Only after the flap is fixed, excise the standing cutaneous deformity created at the end of the rotation, usually in the neck or preauricular area, orienting the scar along a crease or the sternocleidomastoid border. Trim the flap edge to fit the defect rather than stretching the tip into it.
Close over a drain and check perfusion

Achieve careful hemostasis under the wide flap, place a suction drain beneath the neck portion when dissection is extensive, and close in layers. Before leaving the room, check color and capillary refill at the distal leading edge, which is the most vulnerable part of the flap.
cervicofacial-flap.source_label: Cummings 7e Ch 21 (Reconstruction of Facial Defects) and Pasha 6e Ch 8

steps: Secure the airway first

In a stridulous or distressed patient, perform a tracheotomy under local anesthesia while the patient breathes spontaneously, protecting the cervical spine. Avoid blind or repeated translaryngeal intubation through a disrupted larynx. If the patient arrived intubated, assess the mucosa promptly and convert to a tracheotomy within 24 hours when laryngeal injury is significant.
Complete the endoscopic assessment

With the airway secure, perform microlaryngoscopy with tracheoscopy, direct pharyngoscopy and esophagoscopy. Map lacerations, exposed cartilage, anterior commissure disruption and hematomas, and palpate each arytenoid to separate cricoarytenoid dislocation from neural immobility. Look specifically for a pharyngoesophageal tear from a displaced thyroid cornu.
Treat what you can from above

Small lacerations, hematomas and a dislocated cricoarytenoid joint can often be handled endoscopically by drainage, suture or closed reduction. If the framework is stable and the endolarynx essentially intact, stop here and manage with observation, reflux and edema control and serial flexible endoscopy rather than open exploration.
Expose the framework

Make a transverse skin incision over the cricoid, raise subplatysmal flaps to the hyoid and toward the sternal notch, and separate the strap muscles in the midline. Expose the thyroid and cricoid cartilages while preserving the outer perichondrium, which holds fragments together and later anchors the anterior commissure.
Repair laryngotracheal separation

If the cricoid and trachea are separated, find the trachea, which retracts toward the mediastinum, and secure the airway through it if not already done. Debride devitalized edges and perform a primary end-to-end anastomosis. Look for both recurrent laryngeal nerves, which are often injured in this pattern, and record their status.
Decide whether to open the larynx

If fractures are unstable but endolaryngeal injury is minimal or already treated endoscopically, reduce and fix the framework without a thyrotomy. Open the larynx for anterior commissure disruption, large or deep lacerations, exposed cartilage or mucosal loss that cannot be closed from above.
Perform the laryngofissure

Enter through a vertical midline thyrotomy, dividing exactly through the anterior commissure, or use a paramedian fracture line close to the midline. Retract the alae with sutures or hooks, evacuate hematomas, and inspect the whole endolarynx to plan the mucosal repair.
Repair the mucosa

Close lacerations with 5-0 or 6-0 absorbable sutures so no cartilage remains exposed to the airway, debriding only clearly devitalized tissue. Cover mucosal loss with local advancement flaps; posterior commissure defects should be reconstructed with piriform, supraglottic or postcricoid mucosal advancement to prevent posterior glottic stenosis.
Address the arytenoid and epiglottis

Reduce a dislocated arytenoid onto its cricoid facet under direct vision, and remove it only when it is severely disrupted and nonviable. Resuspend an avulsed epiglottic petiole to the thyroid cartilage, or excise a nonviable epiglottis, so it cannot prolapse into the airway.
Restore the anterior commissure

Reattach the anterior ends of both vocal folds to the anterior thyroid cartilage or its outer perichondrium with a slowly absorbable monofilament suture, at matching levels on each side. Restoring correct vocal fold height and a sharp anterior commissure is the key to voice outcome.
Stent only when needed

Place a soft silastic stent for comminuted framework that will not hold its shape or for raw opposing surfaces likely to web; a keel suffices for isolated anterior commissure mucosal injury. Secure it with a 2-0 polypropylene suture through stent and framework, tied over the larynx, remembering that stents add granulation and mucosal injury.
Reduce and fix the fractures

Reduce thyroid fractures to restore laryngeal height and width and fix them with low-profile titanium or resorbable miniplates, keeping screws out of the endolarynx. The cricoid arch rarely fully calcifies and can usually be repaired with sutures alone. Close the perichondrium and reapproximate the strap muscles.
Close and reinspect

Close in layers over a drain, secure the tracheostomy tube, and reinspect the larynx endoscopically to confirm stent position, airway lumen and hemostasis. Explore a recurrent laryngeal nerve only if transection is evident or later electromyography confirms complete palsy, and document the stent removal and first endoscopy plan.

postop: After repair, monitor for delayed edema, hematoma, airway compromise and infection of exposed cartilage. Persistent dysphonia, aspiration, vocal-fold immobility or airway narrowing should prompt endoscopic reassessment for malposition, joint fixation, granulation or evolving stenosis because functional deficits may declare themselves after the acute swelling resolves.
Keep the head elevated, give reflux suppression, and manage the tracheostomy until the airway has been confirmed endoscopically; remove a stent endoscopically at about 10 to 14 days.
Begin oral intake only after swallowing is assessed, especially after arytenoid or supraglottic injury.
attending_followup: Which Schaefer groups need open repair, and when?

Groups III and IV (displaced or unstable fractures, exposed cartilage, large lacerations, anterior commissure disruption) need exploration and repair once the airway is secured, ideally within 24 hours, because delay lets granulation and scar progress to stenosis. Group V (laryngotracheal separation) needs emergency airway control and primary anastomosis.
What is the airway principle in suspected major laryngeal trauma?

Preserve spontaneous ventilation, avoid repeated blind attempts and secure the airway with an experienced multidisciplinary plan—often awake tracheostomy when anatomy is disrupted; carefully selected fiberoptic intubation is not universally safe.
How do arytenoid dislocation and RLN injury differ?

Direct palpation assesses mechanical fixation/malposition and LEMG assesses innervation. Reduction may help dislocation; neural injury follows recovery/prognostic and later reanimation/medialization pathways.

steps: Confirm object, level and urgency

Review frontal and lateral films just before induction, because coins migrate. Exclude a button battery by the double-ring or halo sign on the frontal view and step-off on the lateral view. A battery, sharp object, magnets or complete obstruction goes straight to removal; for a stable smooth coin, repeat the film in the holding area.
Plan anesthesia and protect the airway

Agree the plan with anesthesia beforehand. Intubate for most esophageal foreign bodies to prevent aspiration on removal and limit tracheal compression by the scope, using rapid sequence induction when secretions pool. Avoid cricoid pressure with a large or sharp proximal object, and watch for a high object dislodging into the airway.
Choose the instrument and rehearse

Use rigid esophagoscopy for proximal, sharp or complex objects and whenever airway control and fine manipulation matter; flexible endoscopy suits smooth distal objects and those needing gastric access. Select the largest esophagoscope that passes easily, test light and suction, and try the forceps on a duplicate object on the back table.
Inspect the hypopharynx first

Perform direct laryngoscopy and inspect the hypopharynx and esophageal inlet before inserting the esophagoscope. An object sitting at the cricopharyngeus can sometimes be seen and removed directly with Magill forceps, avoiding esophagoscopy, but do not grope blindly in the hypopharynx.
Insert the esophagoscope

With the patient supine in a neutral sniffing position and the cervical spine straight, protect the upper teeth or gums and pass the scope behind the arytenoids through the cricopharyngeus with the lumen centered. Advance only under direct vision, and never pass rigid instruments blindly beyond the object or an area of injury.
Assess the object in place

Clear secretions and look before grasping: note orientation, impaction depth, edema, ulceration and any granulation hiding an edge. For a sharp object find the point, for a coin find its edge, and for a food bolus look for an underlying stricture or the rings and furrows of eosinophilic esophagitis.
Grasp with the right forceps

Match forceps to the object: coin or alligator forceps for coins, rat-tooth or optical alligator forceps for irregular objects, and peanut forceps for rounded ones. Grasp a stable edge firmly, and if the object will not fit through the scope, draw it against the tip and withdraw object, forceps and scope together as one unit.
Manage sharp objects safely

A leading point perforates while a trailing point does not. Free a buried point from the wall, rotate the object so the point trails, and draw the point into the tip of the largest scope or under a flexible protector hood or overtube before withdrawing. If the object cannot be sheathed safely, stop and plan an open or combined approach.
Handle a food bolus

Remove a food bolus piecemeal with forceps or a net, or advance it gently into the stomach with a flexible scope only after the lumen beyond is seen to be clear. Never use meat-dissolving agents. Take biopsies from at least two levels of the esophagus at the same sitting to look for eosinophilic esophagitis, even if the mucosa looks normal.
Remove a button battery as an emergency

Remove the battery at once, since injury progresses by the minute. Note which way the negative pole (the narrower side) faced, because the worst burn lies there, and grade the injury. If there is no perforation, irrigate the site with 50 to 150 mL of 0.25% sterile acetic acid, and plan a second look in 2 to 4 days for deep injury.
Re-examine the whole esophagus

Reinsert the scope after removal to inspect the impaction site for laceration, deep ulceration or perforation and to look for retained fragments or a second object, then survey the rest of the esophagus. Record depth from the incisors. If perforation is suspected, stop instrumenting and image rather than probing the defect.
Set the postoperative plan

Match diet and imaging to the injury: mucosal abrasion alone can resume diet after recovery, while deep ulceration, battery injury or suspected perforation stays NPO pending a contrast study or CT. Obtain a film after a difficult extraction, and watch for fever, tachycardia and tachypnea as early signs of mediastinitis.

fields.indications: An impacted esophageal foreign body or food bolus. Emergent removal for a button battery, sharp or pointed object, magnets, complete obstruction with inability to handle secretions, or signs of perforation; urgent removal (within about 24 hours) for other retained objects. An asymptomatic older child with a smooth mid or distal esophageal coin swallowed within the past 24 hours and no esophageal disease may be observed for about 8 to 16 hours with a repeat film; remove without waiting for a proximal coin, symptoms, a young child or an unknown or longer ingestion time. Always check the film for a button battery (double ring or step-off), and biopsy for eosinophilic esophagitis at food bolus removal.

steps: Confirm the cleft under anesthesia

Under total intravenous anesthesia with spontaneous ventilation and topical lidocaine, suspend the larynx and palpate the interarytenoid region with a probe, spreading the arytenoids to define the cleft's lowest point relative to the vocal folds and cricoid. Classify by Benjamin-Inglis type, and complete bronchoscopy and esophagoscopy for fistula, malacia and other causes of aspiration.
Choose the approach

For a type 1 cleft, consider interarytenoid injection augmentation as a diagnostic and temporizing step. Repair type 1, most type 2 and limited type 3 clefts endoscopically when exposure is excellent and comorbidity is low. Most type 3 and all type 4 clefts need open repair with planned postoperative airway support and enteral access.
Set up endoscopic exposure

Center the interarytenoid area in the field with a suspension laryngoscope and operating microscope, using a vocal fold retractor to spread the arytenoids. Have microlaryngeal needle holders, alligator forceps, scissors and a knot pusher ready, and agree a rescue plan with anesthesia for jet ventilation or intermittent intubation.
Denude the cleft edges

Remove the mucosa along both edges of the cleft with CO2 laser, cold instruments or both, creating raw surfaces broad enough to heal together while preserving the arytenoid cartilages. Remove every trace of mucosa at the apex, because residual epithelium there is the usual cause of a persistent interarytenoid fistula.
Close from the apex upward

Place the deepest suture first, right at the apex, using fine absorbable suture (4-0 to 7-0 polyglactin or polydioxanone by patient size) tied with a knot pusher. Add further sutures upward until the closure reaches normal interarytenoid height, approximating the denuded surfaces without tearing them.
Avoid overtightening the larynx

Check that the closure has not crowded the arytenoids or narrowed the posterior glottis. If redundant arytenoid mucosa or laryngomalacia would obstruct, add a supraglottoplasty dividing the aryepiglottic folds or a corniculate pexy. Suction blood and secretions before releasing suspension.
Prepare for open repair

For long clefts, optimize reflux and lung disease first, place a tracheotomy or plan a nasotracheal tube to avoid prolonged positive pressure on the repair, and arrange enteral access, preferably a gastrostomy rather than a nasogastric tube against the suture line. Involve thoracic surgery when the cleft reaches the thoracic trachea, where ECMO or bypass may be needed.
Open the anterior airway

Through a horizontal neck incision, separate the strap muscles and perform a midline laryngofissure through the inferior thyroid cartilage, cricoid and upper tracheal rings, adding a partial sternotomy for distal extension. This anterior approach exposes the whole cleft while staying away from the recurrent laryngeal nerves lateral to the posterior framework.
Raise the mucosal flaps

Incise along the mucosal edges of the cleft on each side to separate an airway layer from a pharyngoesophageal layer, ideally with asymmetric flaps so the two suture lines will not overlie each other. Free enough tissue for tension-free closure while keeping the dissection in the midline posterior wall.
Close the pharyngoesophageal layer

Close the esophageal flaps first with interrupted 5-0 or 6-0 absorbable sutures, forming a watertight wall that does not narrow the esophageal lumen. If the lumen is in doubt, check it against an esophageal bougie of suitable size before tying the final sutures.
Interpose tissue

Lay an interposition graft over the esophageal closure, such as tibial periosteum, pericardium, auricular cartilage, or a strap or sternocleidomastoid muscle flap, and fix it laterally so it cannot curl or slip. This third layer separates the suture lines and lowers the risk of recurrent fistula.
Close the airway layer and the fissure

Close the posterior laryngotracheal mucosa over the graft as a separate layer, keeping the posterior glottis and subglottis wide. Secure the tracheostomy or nasotracheal tube, then close the laryngofissure and tracheofissure, reapproximating the anterior commissure precisely, and close the neck over a drain.
Plan airway and feeding recovery

After endoscopic repair, observe the child 1 to 3 days in a monitored bed. After open repair, keep the child intubated or on the tracheostomy in intensive care for several days, repeat laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy to check the repair before extubation, and continue tube feeds for weeks until a swallow study allows oral intake.
laryngotracheal-cleft-repair.source_label: Cummings 7e Ch 214 (Laryngotracheal Clefts) and Bluestone Ch 89

fields.indications: Symptomatic posterior laryngeal or laryngotracheoesophageal cleft with aspiration, feeding difficulty or pulmonary morbidity (recurrent pneumonia, respiratory admissions, frequent steroid courses) that persists despite thickened feeds, feeding therapy and reflux treatment, when the aspiration is not mainly explained by neuromuscular or syndromic disease. Clefts that extend below the vocal folds (type 2 and deeper) need repair in nearly all cases; type 1 clefts are repaired when conservative care or injection augmentation fails.
setup: Before repair, make the postoperative airway and feeding plan explicit: intended extubation versus protected intubation, enteral access, timing of oral intake, and the planned swallow/endoscopic reassessment should reflect cleft depth, pulmonary disease, aspiration burden and whether the repair is endoscopic or open.

Define cleft type/length and aspiration physiology before repair using endoscopic assessment plus swallow/feeding history; review pulmonary morbidity, reflux/esophageal disease and prior feeding interventions, because limited type I disease may be managed differently from deeper clefts and larger defects require a deliberate open-versus-endoscopic and postoperative airway/feeding plan.

Review the functional swallow study or FEES for thin-liquid aspiration, and the prior endoscopy with interarytenoid palpation and Benjamin-Inglis type; type 1, most type 2 and limited type 3 clefts with good exposure are repaired endoscopically, while most type 3 and all type 4 clefts need an open approach.
Coordinate airway/anesthesia and exposure strategy; protect dentition and document baseline voice/airway/swallow function.
attending_followup: Why is swallow imaging not enough to classify the cleft?
It demonstrates aspiration physiology but not the exact posterior anatomic depth; operative inspection/palpation defines the lesion.
When might injection augmentation be considered?

For a type 1 cleft or shallow interarytenoid deficiency, inject 0.2 to 0.6 mL of a temporary filler such as carboxymethylcellulose into the interarytenoid notch at the diagnostic laryngoscopy. Improved aspiration supports the diagnosis and predicts benefit from definitive repair; the effect lasts about 3 months on average, and some children need nothing further.
Is the closure layered in both endoscopic and open repair?

No. Endoscopic repair approximates the denuded cleft edges as one closure, so complete removal of mucosa at the apex and a secure deepest suture are what prevent a fistula. Open repair of long clefts must recreate separate airway and esophageal walls with at least two layers, ideally with interposed tissue and offset suture lines, to limit dehiscence and recurrent fistula.

steps: Select and prepare the patient

Confirm an indication within the reach of the scope and that the patient can tolerate an awake procedure. Check for the more patent nostril, anticoagulation and a history of vasovagal episodes, and ask the patient to take nothing by mouth for about 3 hours beforehand to reduce regurgitation and aspiration.
Anesthetize and decongest the nose

Spray the more patent side with an atomized mixture of oxymetazoline and 4% lidocaine or 2% tetracaine, adding soaked pledgets for 5 to 10 minutes in a tight nose. Spray the oropharynx lightly or have the patient gargle viscous lidocaine, avoiding excess hypopharyngeal anesthesia, which causes pooled secretions and coughing.
Position the patient and check the scope

Seat the patient upright, leaning forward at the waist with the neck extended, with the monitor in your line of sight. Check the air, water and suction functions and the working channel of the roughly 5 mm scope, lubricate the shaft, and have biopsy forceps and specimen pots ready.
Pass the nose and examine the upper airway

Advance along the nasal floor beneath the inferior turbinate, or between turbinate and septum if the floor is narrow, with the patient breathing through the nose to open the velopharynx. Examine the nasopharynx, oropharynx, hypopharynx and larynx, including vocal fold motion, before going further.
Enter the esophagus

Have the patient tuck the chin to flex the neck, hold the tip just above the postcricoid area or at the piriform sinus, and ask for a swallow. Follow the opening cricopharyngeus with gentle pressure and the lumen in view; resistance may mean a tight sphincter or a Zenker diverticulum, so never push blindly.
Advance through the esophagus

Insufflate only enough to see the lumen and advance with it centered, noting distances from the nasal ala: upper esophagus about 18 cm, aortic impression 24 to 26 cm, left mainstem bronchus 29 to 30 cm and diaphragmatic pinch 41 to 43 cm. Record lesions, rings, strictures and motility as the patient swallows.
Inspect the gastroesophageal junction

Identify the Z-line, where gray-white squamous mucosa meets salmon-colored columnar mucosa, and the top of the gastric folds marking the gastroesophageal junction; these should coincide. Columnar mucosa above the gastric folds suggests Barrett esophagus, and gastric folds more than 2 cm above the diaphragmatic pinch indicate a hiatal hernia.
Retroflex in the stomach

When indicated, enter the stomach, insufflate, and retroflex by rotating the scope 180 degrees and fully deflecting the tip to view the cardia and the scope at the hiatus, looking for a sliding or paraesophageal hernia. Suction the gastric air before straightening the tip and withdrawing to limit discomfort.
Take biopsies

Stabilize the scope, pass forceps through the working channel and sample under direct vision: targeted biopsies of masses or irregular mucosa, multiple biopsies of suspected Barrett mucosa, and at least six biopsies from two or more levels for suspected eosinophilic esophagitis. Avoid biopsy over a pulsatile extrinsic impression.
Dilate only along a clear axis

If a stricture needs dilation, pass a guidewire through the channel beyond it, withdraw the scope over the wire, reinsert the scope beside the wire, and pass the balloon over the wire so inflation is watched endoscopically. Size up in steps, hold each inflation about a minute, and stop for pain or bleeding out of proportion.
Withdraw with a second look

Withdraw slowly while insufflating, rechecking the distal esophagus and biopsy sites for bleeding or a mucosal tear. Give a burst of air at the upper sphincter on the way out, because the postcricoid region is the hardest area to see fully, then recheck the pharynx and nasal passage.
Discharge safely

Keep the patient NPO for 60 to 90 minutes until throat anesthesia wears off. Document findings by distance from the nasal ala, biopsy sites and any dilation size, and advise urgent return for chest or neck pain, fever, breathing difficulty, vomiting blood or inability to swallow saliva.
transnasal-esophagoscopy.source_label: Cummings 7e Ch 69 (Transnasal Esophagoscopy) and Atlas of Head and Neck Surgery (Simo, Pracy, Fernandes 2024)

fields.indications: Awake office evaluation of the pharynx, esophagus and proximal stomach in a patient who can tolerate unsedated endoscopy and has one adequately patent nasal passage. Esophageal indications include dysphagia, reflux symptoms despite therapy, long-standing reflux, Barrett screening or surveillance and biopsy of radiographic abnormalities; extraesophageal indications include chronic cough, globus, laryngopharyngeal reflux and evaluation or biopsy for head and neck cancer. It also supports office procedures such as balloon dilation and tracheoesophageal puncture.
attending_followup: What is TNE best at?

Unsedated office evaluation and biopsy of the pharynx, esophagus and gastroesophageal junction, for example for dysphagia, Barrett screening or a head and neck cancer workup. Avoiding sedation removes the cause of over half of conventional endoscopy adverse events, and hemodynamic swings are smaller than with transoral endoscopy.
When should you stop and escalate?
Unexpected resistance, poor tolerance, inadequate visualization or a problem requiring therapeutic GI endoscopy.
What patient factor is most likely to make TNE technically difficult or unsafe?

Severe nasal obstruction/septal deviation, an overactive gag reflex, or poor patient cooperation can prevent adequate unsedated passage and visualization, in which case escalation to sedated or operative endoscopy is appropriate.
